<!-- introtheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{introtheorem: General Cuntz Krieger}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. Suppose that there exists a vertex $v \in E^0$ such that $v$ either supports a single loop or supports multiple cycles and every vertex in $E$ admits a finite path to $v$. Let $$H = \{ x \in E^0 \; \vert \; \text{$v$ does not admit a finite path to $x$} \}$$ so that $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$ is an ideal of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. The Cuntz semigroup of $C^*(E)$ is isomorphic to the stack of the Cuntz semigroup of the quotient $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash H))$ above the Cuntz semigroup of the ideal $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$.
<!-- end introtheorem-1 -->
<!-- introtheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions \ref{property: S1}, \ref{property: S2} and \ref{property: S3}. Place a copy of $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ at every source vertex in $E$, a copy of $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ at every vertex supporting a single loop and a copy of $\{ 0, \infty \}$ at every vertex supporting more than one cycle. The Cuntz semigroup of $C^*(E)$ is generated by these copies of $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$, $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ and $\{ 0, \infty \}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
When restricted to each individual disjoint component, the addition and order are the usual ones. Across components, the elements of the Cuntz semigroups at every vertex are subject to the following relations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $v, w$ are vertices in $E$ and $w$ admits a finite path to $v$, then a non-zero Cuntz class coming from the Cuntz semigroup at $v$ absorbs any Cuntz class coming from the Cuntz semigroup at $w$. 
\item If $v$ is a vertex in $E$ and $\{ x_1, \dots, x_n \}$ is the set of vertices distinct from $v$ which emit an edge to $v$, then the sum of the largest elements of the Cuntz semigroups at $x_1, \dots, x_n$ is equal to the zero element of the Cuntz semigroup at $v$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end introtheorem-2 -->
<!-- introcorollary-1: body_md -->
\label{introcorollary: Cu E One Comparison}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ has the 1-comparison property. In particular, if $F$ is an arbitrary finite graph, then $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F))$ has the 1-comparison property.
<!-- end introcorollary-1 -->
<!-- introtheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{introtheorem: Covering Dimension}
Let $E$ be an arbitrary graph. Then $\dim \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \leq 1$. Moreover, if $E$ satisfies Condition (K), then $\dim \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) = 0$.
<!-- end introtheorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $S$ be a positively ordered monoid. $S$ is said to be a \textbf{Cu-semigroup} if $S$ satisfies the following four axioms:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(O1)}[axiom: O1]}] Every increasing sequence in $S$ has a supremum.
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(O2)}[axiom: O2]}] If $s \in S$ then there exists a sequence $\{ s_n \}_{n > 0}$ in $S$ such that $s_m \ll s_{m+1}$ for $m > 0$ and  $s = \sup_{n > 0} s_n$.
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(O3)}[axiom: O3]}] If $x, x', y, y' \in S$, $x' \ll x$ and $y' \ll y$ then $x' + y' \ll x + y$. 
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(O4)}[axiom: O4]}] If $\{ f_n \}_{n > 0}$ and $\{ g_n \}_{n > 0}$ are increasing sequences in $S$ then $${\sup}_{n > 0} \; f_n + {\sup}_{n > 0} \; g_n = {\sup}_{n > 0} \; (f_n + g_n).$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra and $a, b \in A_+$. The element $a$ is \textbf{Cuntz subequivalent} to or Cuntz below $b$ (denoted by $a \precsim b$) if for $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $r \in A$ such that $\lVert a - r b r^* \rVert < \epsilon$. Moreover, $a$ is \textbf{Cuntz equivalent} to $b$ (denoted by $a \sim b$) if $a \precsim b$ and $b \precsim a$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
The \textbf{Cuntz semigroup} of $A$, denoted by $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$, is defined to be the set
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}(A) = (A \otimes K)_+ / \sim \; = \{ [a] \; \vert \; a \in (A \otimes K)_+ \}.
\end{equation*}
If $[a], [b] \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ then the partial order and addition on $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$ are given respectively by setting $[a] \leq [b]$ if and only if $a \precsim b$ and
\begin{equation*}
[a] + [b] = [a \oplus b] = \left[ 
\begin{pmatrix}
a & 0 \\
0 & b
\end{pmatrix}
\right].
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $S$ be a Cu-semigroup and $I$ be a submonoid of $S$. $I$ is said to be an \textbf{ideal} of $S$ if it satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $I$ is downwards-hereditary. That is, if $x, y \in S$, $x \leq y$ and $y \in I$ then $x \in I$.
\item $I$ is closed under suprema of increasing sequences. That is, if $\{ x_n \}_{n > 0}$ is an increasing sequence in $I$ then its supremum must also lie in $I$.
\end{enumerate}
The lattice of ideals of $S$ is denoted by $\operatorname{Lat}(S)$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{definition: Countably Based}
A Cu-semigroup $S$ is said to be \textbf{countably based} if there exists a countable subset $X \subseteq S$ such that every element in $S$ is the supremum of a rapidly increasing sequence of elements in $X$. Such a subset $X$, if it exists, is called \textbf{sup-dense} in $S$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Countably Based}
Let $A$ be a separable C*-algebra and $X$ be a countable dense subset of $A_+$. If $a, b \in A_+$ and $[a] \ll [b]$ then there exists $x \in X$ and $m > 0$ such that in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$,
\begin{equation*}
[a] \ll \Big[ \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \ll [b].
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Sandwich}
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra, $x \in \Sigma_A$ and $x' \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ be such that $x' \ll x$. Then there exists $a \in A_+$ such that $x' \ll [a] \ll x$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem: CRS}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r, "\iota"] & A \arrow[r, "\pi"] & A/I \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be an extension of C*-algebras and suppose that $I$ is a $\sigma$-unital ideal of $A$. The induced sequence of positively ordered monoids
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & \operatorname{Cu}(I) \arrow[r, "\operatorname{Cu}(\iota)"] & \operatorname{Cu}(A) \arrow[r, "\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)"] & \operatorname{Cu}(A/I) \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
is short exact. Furthermore, if $x, y \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(x) \leq \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(y)$ then there exists $z \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ such that $x \leq y + z$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{definition: Quotient Cu Semigroup}
 Let $S$ be a Cu-semigroup and $I$ be an ideal of $S$. If $a, b \in S$ then we say $a \leq_I b$ if and only if there exists $i \in I$ such that $a \leq b + i$. Define an equivalence relation $\sim_I$ by setting $a \sim_I b$ if and only if $a \leq_I b$ and $b \leq_I a$. The \textbf{quotient Cu-semigroup} $S/I$ is given by the set
\begin{equation*}
S/I = S/\sim_I \; = \{ [s]_I \; \vert \; s \in S \}.
\end{equation*}
The partial order on $S/I$ is given by $[a]_I \leq [b]_I$ if and only if $a \leq_I b$ in $S$ and addition is given by $[a]_I + [b]_I = [a + b]_I$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Refined Moves Stable Iso}
Let $E$ and $F$ be finite graphs and suppose that $F$ is obtained by applying a sequence of the moves (O), (I-), (CO) and (S) to $E$. Then $C^*(E) \otimes K \cong C^*(F) \otimes K$. In particular, $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F))$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{definition: O}
Let $E$ be a graph with finitely many vertices and $w \in E^0$ be a vertex that is not a source. Partition the set $r^{-1}(w)$ into a disjoint union of finitely many non-empty sets so that
\begin{equation*}
r^{-1}(w) = \mathcal{E}_1 \sqcup \mathcal{E}_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup \mathcal{E}_n
\end{equation*}
and at most one of the $\mathcal{E}_i$ has infinite cardinality. Define the graph $E_O$ by
\begin{equation*}
E_O^0 = \{ v^1 \; \vert \; \text{$v \in E^0$ and $v \neq w$} \} \cup \{ w^1, \dots, w^n \},
\end{equation*} 
\begin{equation*}
E_O^1 = \{ e^1 \; \vert \; \text{$e \in E^1$ and $s(e) \neq w$} \} \cup \{ e^1, \dots, e^n \; \vert \; \text{$e \in E^1$ and $s(e) = w$} \},
\end{equation*}
\vspace{-1 mm}
\begin{equation*}
s_O(e^i) = 
\begin{cases}
s(e)^1, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $s(e) \neq w$,} \\
w^i, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $s(e) = w$.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*} \vspace{1 mm}
\begin{equation*}
r_O(e^i) = 
\begin{cases}
r(e)^1, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $r(e) \neq w$,} \\
r(e)^j, \text{ if $e \in E^1$, $r(e) = w$ and $e \in \mathcal{E}_j$.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
The graph $E_O$ is said to be obtained by applying move (O) to $E$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{definition: I-}
Let $E$ be a graph with finitely many vertices and $w \in E^0$ be a regular vertex (not a source or an infinite receiver). Partition the set $s^{-1}(w)$ into a disjoint union of finitely many sets (some of which could be empty) so that
\begin{equation*}
s^{-1}(w) = \mathcal{E}_1 \sqcup \mathcal{E}_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup \mathcal{E}_n.
\end{equation*}
Define the graph $E_I$ by
\begin{equation*}
E_I^0 = \{ v^1 \; \vert \; \text{$v \in E^0$ and $v \neq w$} \} \cup \{ w^1, \dots, w^n \},
\end{equation*} 
\begin{equation*}
E_I^1 = \{ e^1 \; \vert \; \text{$e \in E^1$ and $r(e) \neq w$} \} \cup \{ e^1, \dots, e^n \; \vert \; \text{$e \in E^1$ and $r(e) = w$} \},
\end{equation*} \vspace{-1 mm}
\begin{equation*}
s_I(e^i) = 
\begin{cases}
s(e)^1, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $s(e) \neq w$,} \\
w^j, \text{ if $e \in E^1$, $s(e) = w$ and $e \in \mathcal{E}_j$.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*} \vspace{1 mm}
\begin{equation*}
r_I(e^i) = 
\begin{cases}
r(e)^1, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $r(e) \neq w$,} \\
w^i, \text{ if $e \in E^1$ and $r(e) = w$.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
The graph $E_I$ is said to be obtained by applying move (I-) to $E$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{definition: S}
Let $E$ be a a graph with finitely many vertices and $w \in E^0$ be a regular sink. Define the graph $E_S$ by
\begin{equation*}
E_S^0 = E^0 \backslash \{ w \}, \quad E_S^1 = E^1 \backslash r^{-1}(w), \quad s_S = s \vert_{E_S^1} \quad \text{and} \quad r_S = r \vert_{E_S^1}. 
\end{equation*}
The graph $E_S$ is said to be obtained by applying move (S) to $E$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{definition: CO}
Let $E$ be a graph with finitely many vertices and $w \in E^0$ be a regular vertex which does not support a loop. Define the graph $E_{\text{CO}}$ by $E_{\text{CO}}^0 = E^0 \backslash \{ w \}$ and
\begin{equation*}
E_{\text{CO}}^1 = \big(E^1 \backslash (s^{-1}(w) \cup r^{-1}(w)) \big) \; \sqcup \;  \{ [ef] \; \vert \; e \in s^{-1}(w), \; f \in r^{-1}(w) \}.
\end{equation*}
The source and range maps of $E_{\text{CO}}$ extend those of $E$ and satisfy
\begin{equation*}
s_{\text{CO}}([ef]) = s(f) \qquad \text{and} \qquad  \quad r_{\text{CO}}([ef]) = r(e). 
\end{equation*}
The graph $E_{\text{CO}}$ is said to be obtained by applying move (CO) to $E$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let $E$ be a row-finite graph. The graph C*-algebra $C^*(E)$ is said to be \textbf{gauge-simple} if the only gauge-invariant ideals of $C^*(E)$ are $\{ 0 \}$ and $C^*(E)$. Equivalently by \eqref{equation: Hereditary Saturated}, the only hereditary, saturated subsets of $E^0$ are $\emptyset$ and $E^0$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Let $E$ be a graph and $M \subseteq E^0$ be non-empty. $M$ is said to be a \textbf{maximal tail} if the following three conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(M1)}[property: M1]}] If $v \in E^0$, $w \in M$ and there exists a path from $w$ to $v$ then $v \in M$.
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(M2)}[property: M2]}] If $v \in M$ and $0 < \lvert r^{-1}(v) \rvert < \infty$ then there exists $e \in E^1 = E$ such that $r(e) = v$ and $s(e) \in M$. 
\item[{\crtcrossreflabel{(M3)}[property: M3]}] If $v, w \in M$ then there exists $y \in M$ such that $y \geq v$ and $y \geq w$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{definition: Maximal Tail Tau}
Let $E$ be a graph. Define $\mathcal{MT}(E)$ to be the set of all maximal tails in $E$. Define $\mathcal{MT}_\gamma(E)$ to be the set of all maximal tails in $E$ such that each cycle in $M$ has an entry in $M$. Finally, define $\mathcal{MT}_\tau(E) = \mathcal{MT}(E) \backslash \mathcal{MT}_\gamma(E)$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{definition: Purely Large Bouwen Gabe}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & A/I \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be an extension of C*-algebras. The extension is said to be \textbf{purely large} if for $y \in I_+$ and $x \in A_+ \backslash I$, $y \precsim x$ in $A$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theorem: Purely Large Tensor Product}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & A/I \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be a purely large extension. Then the stabilised extension
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \otimes K \arrow[r] & A \otimes K \arrow[r] & A/I \otimes K \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
is also purely large.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Assume that $x \in (A \otimes K)_+ \backslash (I \otimes K)$ and let $\pi: A \otimes K \rightarrow A/I \otimes K$ denote the quotient map. We need to show that $x$ Cuntz dominates any positive element in $I \otimes K$. By applying Kirchberg's slice lemma (see \cite[Lemma 2.15]{BK04}), we will first reduce the problem to the special case where $x$ is an elementary tensor. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Since $K$ is nuclear, the minimal tensor product by $K$ is spatially implemented. So there exist faithful representations $A/I \subseteq B(H_{A/I})$ and $K \subseteq B(H_K)$ such that $A/I \otimes K \subseteq B(H_{A/I}) \otimes B(H_K)$. Let $\xi_{A/I}$ and $\xi_K$ be unit cyclic vectors in $H_{A/I}$ and $H_K$ respectively. Let $\phi_{A/I}$ and $\phi_K$ be the functionals induced by $\xi_{A/I}$ and $\xi_K$ respectively. Since $\pi(x) \neq 0$ and our representation of $A/I \otimes K$ onto $B(H_{A/I}) \otimes B(H_K)$ is faithful then
\begin{equation*}
(\phi_{A/I} \otimes \phi_K)(\pi(x)) = \langle \pi(x)(\xi_{A/I} \otimes \xi_K), \xi_{A/I} \otimes \xi_K \rangle = \lVert \pi(x)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\xi_{A/I} \otimes \xi_K) \rVert^2 > 0.  
\end{equation*}
Hence, there exist pure states $\rho_{A/I}$ and $\rho_K$ on $A/I$ and $K$ respectively such that $(\rho_{A/I} \otimes \rho_K)(\pi(x)) > 0$, as otherwise by \cite[Theorem 5.1.8]{Mur90}, $(\eta_{A/I} \otimes \eta_K)(\pi(x)) = 0$ for arbitrary positive linear functionals $\eta_{A/I}$ and $\eta_K$ on $A/I$ and $K$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now let $\rho_A$ be the pure state on $A$ induced from $\rho_{A/I}$. Then $\rho_A(I) = \{ 0 \}$ and $(\rho_A \otimes \rho_K)(x) = (\rho_{A/I} \otimes \rho_K)(\pi(x)) > 0$. By Kirchberg's slice lemma, there exist $z \in (E \otimes K) \backslash \{ 0 \}$, $e \in A_+$ and $d \in K_+$ such that
\begin{equation*}
zz^* \in \overline{x ( A \otimes K) x}, \qquad z^* z = e \otimes d \qquad \text{and} \qquad \rho_E(e) \rho_K(d) > 0.
\end{equation*} 
Observe that $e \in A_+ \backslash I$ and by \cite[Proposition 2.7 (i)]{KR00}, $e \otimes d \sim z z^* \precsim x$. Consequently by Rørdam's lemma (see \cite[Proposition 2.4]{Ror92}), it suffices to show that $e \otimes d$ Cuntz dominates all positive elements of the form $(y - \delta)_+$ where $y \in (I \otimes K)_+$ and $\delta > 0$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
To this end, assume that $y \in (I \otimes K)_+$ and $\delta > 0$. Using approximate units on both $I$ and $K$, there exist $a \in I_+$ and $b \in K_+$ such that 
\begin{equation*}
\lVert (a \otimes b) y (a \otimes b) - y \rVert < \frac{\delta}{2}. 
\end{equation*}
So by choosing $\epsilon > 0$ small enough, we can arrange for
\begin{equation*}
\lVert (a \otimes (b - \epsilon)_+) y (a \otimes (b - \epsilon)_+) - y \rVert < \delta. 
\end{equation*} 
Applying \cite[Lemma 2.5 (ii)]{KR00}, we have $(y - \delta)_+ \precsim a \otimes (b - \epsilon)_+$. Consequently, it suffices to show that if $a \in I_+$, $b \in K_+$ and $\epsilon > 0$ then
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Final Reduction}
a \otimes (b - \epsilon)_+ \precsim e \otimes d. 
\end{equation}
First, since $\operatorname{Cu}(K) \cong \overline{\mathbb{N}}$ is simple then it follows from \cite[Proposition 5.1.10]{APT18} that there exists $n > 0$ large enough such that 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Simplicity Application}
(b - \epsilon)_+ \otimes e_{11} \sim (b - \epsilon)_+ \precsim d \otimes 1_n
\end{equation}
where $1_n$ is the unit of $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $e_{11} \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ is the matrix with a 1 in the top left corner and zeros elsewhere. Now since $E$ is a purely large extension then by \cite[Proposition 4.14]{BG24} and \cite[Proposition 6.10]{CGSTW23}, $I$ is separably stable and so there exists a separable stable C*-subalgebra $C$ of $I$ such that $a \in C$. By stability of $C$, there is a unital embedding of $\mathcal{O}_n$ into the multiplier algebra $\mathcal{M}(C)$, which yields isometries $s_1, \dots, s_n \in \mathcal{M}(C)$ such that if $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ then $$s_i^* s_i = {\sum}_{j = 1}^n s_j s_j^* = 1_{\mathcal{M}(C)}.$$ Now define $a' = \sum_{j = 1}^n s_j a s_j^* \in C_+$ and for $k > 0$, $$v_k = {\sum}_{j = 1}^n s_j a^{\frac{1}{k}} \otimes e_{1j} \in C \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}).$$ By direct computation, $v_k^* (a' \otimes e_{11}) v_k \rightarrow a \otimes 1_n$ as $k \rightarrow \infty$. Hence by Definition \ref{definition: Purely Large Bouwen Gabe}, $a \otimes 1_n \precsim a' \otimes e_{11} \precsim e \otimes e_{11}$. In tandem with \eqref{equation: Simplicity Application}, we have in $(A \otimes K) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ that
\begin{equation*}
a \otimes (b - \epsilon)_+ \otimes e_{11} \precsim a \otimes d \otimes 1_n \precsim e \otimes d \otimes e_{11}. 
\end{equation*}
We obtain the desired Cuntz equivalence in \eqref{equation: Final Reduction}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & A/I \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*} 
be an extension of C*-algebras. The extension is purely large if and only if for $y \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and $x \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$, $y \leq x$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theorem: Kucerovsky Ng}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & A/I \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*} 
be an extension of C*-algebras. Suppose that the ideal $I$ is $\sigma$-unital, stable and satisfies the corona factorisation property. If $A$ is a full extension then it is purely large.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Graph CFP}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. Then $C^*(E)$ and $C^*(E) \otimes K$ have the corona factorisation property.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since every unital graph C*-algebra is built by iteratively taking extensions involving matrix algebras, Kirchberg algebras and C*-algebras stably isomorphic to $C(\mathbb{T})$ then by \cite[Proposition 2.9]{WZ10}, any unital graph C*-algebra must have finite nuclear dimension. By \cite[Corollary 2.8 (i)]{WZ10}, the stabilisation of a unital graph C*-algebra also has finite nuclear dimension. Thus by \cite[Corollary 3.5]{Rob11}, a unital graph C*-algebra and its stabilisation have the corona factorisation property.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theorem: Purely Infinite Properly Infinite}
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra. Then $A$ is purely infinite if and only if every non-zero positive element of $A$ is properly infinite.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma: KR Lemma}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r] & 0 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be an extension of C*-algebras. Assume that all non-zero positive elements in $B$ are properly infinite. If $a \in A_+$ is non-zero, $n \in \{2, 3, \dots \}$ and $\epsilon > 0$ then there exist mutually orthogonal, positive elements $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in \overline{aAa}$ and a positive element $c \in \overline{a I a}$ such that $a_1 \sim a_2 \dots \sim a_n$ and $(a - \epsilon)_+ \precsim a_j \oplus c$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Polar Part Absorbed}
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra, $a \in A_+$ and $p$ be a projection in $A$ such that $p \precsim a$. If $p$ is properly infinite then $a \oplus p \precsim a$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theorem: SR1 Corner Positive Cancellation}
Let $A$ be a unital C*-algebra and $p \in A$ be a projection such that $pAp$ has stable rank one. Let $x, y \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$. If $x + [p] \leq y + [p]$ then $x \leq y$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Dupre Fillmore}
Let $A$ be a unital C*-algebra, $N$ be a (right) Hilbert $A$-module and $M$ be a Hilbert $A$-submodule of $N$. If there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $M$ is a direct summand of $A^n$ then $N = M \oplus M^{\bot}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
First, we prove that if $M$ and $N$ are countably generated (right) Hilbert $A$-modules and $M \oplus pA \cong N \oplus pA$ then $M \cong N$ as Hilbert $A$-modules. Let $\mathcal{B}(M, N)$ denote the set of bounded, adjointable operators from $M = N$; if $M = N$ then we write $\mathcal{B}(M)$ instead of $\mathcal{B}(M, M)$. Let $V: pA \oplus M \rightarrow pA \oplus N$ be an isomorphism of (right) Hilbert $A$-modules. Write $V$ in matrix form so that 
\begin{equation*}
V = 
\begin{pmatrix}
V_{11} & V_{12} \\
V_{21} & V_{22}
\end{pmatrix}
\in 
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathcal{B}(pA) & \mathcal{B}(M, pA) \\
\mathcal{B}(pA, N) & \mathcal{B}(M, N)
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Observe that $\mathcal{B}(pA) \cong pAp$ which has stable rank one by assumption. Hence, by replacing $V_{11}$ with an invertible operator $R \in \mathcal{B}(pA)$ satisfying $\lVert V_{11} - R \rVert < 1$, we may assume without loss of generality that $V$ is an invertible adjointable operator such that $V_{11}$ is itself invertible. By direct computation,
{ \small
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Quasidet Decomp}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{id}_{pA} & 0 \\
- V_{21} V_{11}^{-1} & \text{id}_N
\end{pmatrix}
V
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{id}_{pA} & - V_{11}^{-1} V_{12} \\
0 & \text{id}_M
\end{pmatrix} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
V_{11} & 0 \\
0 & V_{22} - V_{21} V_{11}^{-1} V_{12}
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}}
Since the LHS of \eqref{equation: Quasidet Decomp} is invertible and adjointable, the RHS of \eqref{equation: Quasidet Decomp} is also an invertible adjointable operator from $pA \oplus M$ to $pA \oplus N$. Consequently, $V_{22} - V_{21} V_{11}^{-1} V_{12}$ is an invertible adjointable operator from $M$ to $N$ and by \cite[Proposition 3.8]{Lan95}, $M \cong N$ as Hilbert $A$-modules. Combining this result with Lemma \ref{lemma: Dupre Fillmore}, we see that if $N$ is a countably generated Hilbert $A$-module, $N_1$ and $N_2$ are Hilbert $A$-submodules of $N$ both isomorphic to $pA$ and $pAp$ has stable rank one then $N_1^{\bot} \cong N_2^{\bot}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now let $x = [M]$ and $y = [N]$ where $M$ and $N$ are countably generated (right) Hilbert $A$-modules. Let $E$ be a compactly contained submodule of $M$. Since $pA$ is compactly contained in itself then $E \oplus pA$ is a compactly contained submodule of $M \oplus pA$. Using the assumption that $[M] + [pA] \leq [N] + [pA]$, there exists an embedding $\phi: E \oplus pA \rightarrow N \oplus pA$. Observe that $\phi(\{ 0 \} \oplus pA)$ is a Hilbert submodule of $N \oplus pA$ which is isomorphic to $pA$. So by the previous result, $\phi(\{ 0 \} \oplus pA)^{\bot} \cong N$ as Hilbert $A$-modules. Since $\phi(E \oplus \{ 0 \}) \subseteq \phi(\{ 0 \} \oplus pA)^{\bot}$ then by \cite[Lemma 4.8]{APT11}, $[E] \leq [N]$. By passing to the supremum of all compactly contained submodules of $M$, $[M] \leq [N]$ as required.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{remark: Non Unital SR1 Corner}
It is easy to see that Theorem \ref{theorem: SR1 Corner Positive Cancellation} generalises to the non-unital case. If $A$ is non-unital, then apply Theorem \ref{theorem: SR1 Corner Positive Cancellation} to the minimal unitisation $\tilde{A}$, and use the fact that $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$ is an ideal of $\operatorname{Cu}(\tilde{A})$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{proposition: SR1 Envelope}
Let $A$ be a stable C*-algebra and $a \in A_+$. Then there exist a C*-algebra $B$ and a projection $p_a \in B$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A$ is a closed, two-sided ideal of $B$, 
\item the quotient $B/A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}$ and its unit is the image of $p_a$ in $B/A$,
\item if $x \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ then $x \leq [a]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$ if and only if $x \leq [p_a]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$,
\item as right Hilbert $A$-modules, $p_a A \cong \overline{aA}$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Bounded Projection Cancellation}
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra, $p \in A$ be a projection such that $pAp$ has stable rank one and $x, y, z \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$. If $x + z \ll y + z$ and $z \leq [p]$ then $x \leq y$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By writing $z$ as the supremum of a rapidly increasing sequence, there exists $z' \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ such that $z' \ll z$ and $x + z \leq y + z'$. Recall that the Cuntz semigroup of any C*-algebra satisfies (O5); see \cite[Proposition 4.6]{APT18} for the proof. By applying (O5) to the inequality $z' \ll z \leq [p]$, there exists $c \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ such that $z' + c \leq [p] \leq z + c$. We compute directly that $$x + [p] \leq (x + z) + c \leq y + (z' + c) \leq y + [p].$$ By Remark \ref{remark: Non Unital SR1 Corner}, $x \leq y$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{theorem: General Weak Cancellation}
Let $A$ be a C*-algebra and $x, y \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$. Let $a \in (A \otimes K)_+$ be such that $\overline{a (A \otimes K) a}$ has stable rank one. If $x + [a] \ll y + [a]$ then $x \leq y$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{proposition: SR1 Envelope}, there exist a C*-algebra $B$ and a projection $p_a \in B$ satisfying the listed properties in Proposition \ref{proposition: SR1 Envelope}. In particular, $B$ fits into the extension
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Envelope Extension}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & A \otimes K \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r, "\pi"] & \mathbb{C} \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Since $\overline{a (A \otimes K)} \cong p_a (A \otimes K)$ as right Hilbert $(A \otimes K)$-modules then $\overline{(A \otimes K) a}$ is isomorphic to $(A \otimes K) p_a$ and $$p_a (A \otimes K) p_a = p_a (A \otimes K) \cap (A \otimes K) p_a \cong \overline{a (A \otimes K)} \cap \overline{(A \otimes K) a} = \overline{a (A \otimes K) a}.$$ So by assumption, the hereditary subalgebra $p_a (A \otimes K) p_a$ has stable rank one. Now compress the extension in \eqref{equation: Envelope Extension} by $p_a$ to produce the following extension:
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Compressed Extension}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & p_a (A \otimes K) p_a \arrow[r] & p_a B p_a \arrow[r, "\pi"] & \mathbb{C} \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Note that $\pi(p_a) \mathbb{C} \pi(p_a) = \mathbb{C}$ because the unit of the quotient $B/(A \otimes K) \cong \mathbb{C}$ is $\pi(p_a)$. Since the ideal and quotient of the extension in \eqref{equation: Compressed Extension} both have stable rank one then by \cite[Proposition 4]{LR95}, $p_a B p_a$ must also have stable rank one. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now since $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$ is an ideal of $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$ then $x + [a] \ll y + [a]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: SR1 Envelope}, $[a] \leq [p_a]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$. Hence by Lemma \ref{lemma: Bounded Projection Cancellation}, $x \leq y$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$. Since $x, y \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$, we conclude that $x \leq y$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Collapse Graph}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. Then there exists a finite graph $F$ satisfying the standing assumptions \ref{property: S1}, \ref{property: S2} and \ref{property: S3} such that $C^*(E) \otimes K \cong C^*(F) \otimes K$. In particular, the Cuntz semigroup $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F))$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Assume that $E$ is a finite graph. First, repeatedly apply move (S) to $E$ until $E$ has no regular sinks. Next, suppose that $v \in E^0$ supports a single cycle $\mu$ with length strictly greater than one. We repeatedly apply move (CO) to $\mu$ until it becomes a loop. Finally, we remove all regular transitional vertices from $E$ by applying move (CO) to them. In the end, we obtain a finite graph $F$ satisfying the standing assumptions. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Refined Moves Stable Iso}, $C^*(E)$ and $C^*(F)$ are stably isomorphic.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Suppose that $E$ is the following graph:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (-2, 0) {$a$};
\node (2) at (0, 0) {$b$};
\node (3) at (2, 0) {$c$};
\node (4) at (4, 0) {$d$};
\node (5) at (6, 0) {$e$};
\node (6) at (-4, 0) {$f$};
\node (7) at (0, 2) {$g$};
\draw[->] (2) to (1);
\draw[->] (2) to (3);
\draw[->] (4) to (3);
\draw[->] (5) to (4);
\draw[->] (1) to [bend right = 20] (6);
\draw[->] (6) to [bend right = 20] (1);
\draw[->] (2) to [bend right = 30] (7);
\draw[->] (7) to [bend right = 30] (2);
\draw[->] (1) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation*}
By applying the procedure outlined in the proof of Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph}, we obtain the following graph $F$: 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (-2, 0) {$a$};
\node (2) at (0, 0) {$b$};
\node (5) at (2, 0) {$e$};
\node (6) at (-4, 0) {$f$};
\draw[->] (2) to (1);
\draw[->] (1) to [bend right = 20] (6);
\draw[->] (6) to [bend right = 20] (1);
\draw[->] (1) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (1);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (2);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation*}
It is easy to see that $F$ satisfies the standing assumptions. Note that vertex $e$ does not emit or receive any edges; such a vertex is nevertheless allowed by standing assumption \ref{property: S1} because it is singular. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph}, $C^*(E)$ and $C^*(F)$ are stably isomorphic.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Auto Saturated}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $H \subseteq E^0$. If $H$ is hereditary then it is automatically saturated.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Assume that $E$ is a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $H$ is a hereditary subset of $E^0$. To see that $H$ is saturated, suppose that $v \in E^0$ is such that $0 < \lvert r^{-1}(v) \rvert < \infty$ and $$\{ s(e) \; \vert \; e \in E^1, \; r(e) = v \} \subseteq H.$$ By assumption, $v$ is not a source vertex. Since $E$ satisfies standing assumptions \ref{property: S1} and \ref{property: S2}, $v$ supports at least one cycle. So there exists an edge $f$ such that $r(f) = v$ and $v \geq s(f)$. Now since $s(f) \in H$ and $v \geq s(f)$ then $v \in H$ and $H$ is saturated.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Maximal Tails Standing Assumptions}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then 
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{MT}_\tau(E) = \{ R(v) \; \vert \; \text{$v \in E^0$ supports a single loop} \}. 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
First, assume that $v \in E^0$ supports a single loop. The set $R(v)$ satisfies properties \ref{property: M1} and \ref{property: M3} by definition. Now suppose that $w \in R(v)$ and $0 < \lvert r^{-1}(w) \rvert < \infty$. By the standing assumptions on $E$, $w$ supports at least one cycle and consequently, $R(v)$ satisfies property \ref{property: M2} and is a maximal tail. Moreover, the single loop based at $v$ cannot have an entry lying in $R(v)$ by definition of $R(v)$. So $R(v) \in \mathcal{MT}_\tau(E)$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Conversely, assume that $M \in \mathcal{MT}_\tau(E)$. By \cite[Lemma 2.1]{HS04}, there exist $v \in M$ and a cycle $\mu = \mu_m \dots \mu_2 \mu_1$ based at $v$ which has no entries in $M$; that is, if $e \in E^1$ does not lie on $\mu$ and $r(e)$ lies on $\mu$ then $s(e) \not \in M$. By standing assumption \ref{property: S3}, $m = 1$ and since $\mu$ has no entries in $M$ then it must be the unique cycle based at $v$. Using \cite[Lemma 2.1]{HS04} once more, we have
\begin{equation*}
E^0 \backslash M = \big\{ x \in E^0 \backslash \{ v \} \; \vert \; v \not \geq x \big\} = E^0 \backslash R(v). 
\end{equation*}
So $M = R(v)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{definition: Primitive Non Gauge Invariant}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $v \in E^0$ be a vertex supporting a single loop $g$. Let $t \in \mathbb{T}$. Define $\mathcal{R}_{v, t}$ to be the primitive non-gauge-invariant ideal generated by the gauge-invariant ideal $I_{E^0 \backslash R(v)}$ and $s_g - t p_v$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
More generally, let $K \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ be closed. Define $\mathcal{R}_{v, K}$ to be the non-gauge-invariant ideal $$\mathcal{R}_{v, K} = {\bigcap}_{t \in K} \mathcal{R}_{v, t}.$$
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{definition: Strictly Positive}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $v \in E^0$ support a single loop. Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ be open. If $U$ is non-empty and proper then define $h_{v, U}$ to be a strictly positive element of the ideal $I_{L(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}$. Otherwise, define
\begin{equation*}
h_{v, \emptyset} = {\sum}_{w \in L(v) \backslash \{ v \}} p_w \qquad \text{and} \qquad h_{v, \mathbb{T}} = {\sum}_{w \in L(v)} p_w. 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{definition: QDS}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. The \textbf{quantum double suspension} of $E$, denoted by $S^2 E$, is the finite graph given by connecting all vertices $w \in E^0$ with a single edge $f_w$ to a new vertex $v$ supporting a single loop $g$ so that the vertices and edges of $S^2 E$ are
\begin{equation*}
(S^2 E)^0 = E^0 \cup \{ v \} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (S^2 E)^1 = E^1 \cup \{ f_w \; \vert \; w \in E^0 \} \cup \{ g \}
\end{equation*}
respectively. Furthermore, the source and range maps of $S^2 E$ extend those of $E$ and satisfy
\begin{equation*}
s_{S^2 E}(e) = 
\begin{cases}
w, \text{ if $w \in E^0$ and $e = f_w$,} \\
v, \text{ if $e = g$,}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
r_{S^2 E}(e) = 
\begin{cases}
v, \text{ if $w \in E^0$ and $e = f_w$,} \\
v, \text{ if $e = g$}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
respectively.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{proposition: QDS Forcing}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and suppose that there exists $v \in E^0$ such that $v$ supports a single loop and if $w \in E^0$ then $w \geq v$. Let $H = E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$. Then there exists a finite graph $F$ such that $C^*(E) \otimes K \cong C^*(S^2 F) \otimes K$ and $C^*(H) \otimes K \cong C^*(F) \otimes K$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We first modify $E$ so that every vertex in $E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ emits at least one edge to $v$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
\textbf{Step 1: Introducing edges to $v$.} \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Assume that $w \in E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ emits edges to $v$. If $w$ does not receive any edges, then $w$ is a source vertex and there is nothing to do. If $w$ receives edges then there are two cases to consider. First suppose that $w$ does not support a loop. By applying move (CO) to the vertex $w$, we produce in the resulting graph edges whose sources lie in the set $\{ s(e) \; \vert \; e \in E^1, \; r(e) = w \}$ and whose ranges are $v$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now if $w$ supports at least one loop, then let $L_w$ be the set of all loops based at $w$. We apply move (I-) to the vertex $w$ with the following partition of $s^{-1}(w)$:
\begin{equation} \label{equation: QDS I- Partition}
s^{-1}(w) = L_w \sqcup \big(s^{-1}(w) \backslash L_w \big).
\end{equation}
The vertex $w$ is replaced with two vertices $w_1$ and $w_2$. There are $k$ loops based at $w_1$ and $k$ edges from $w_1$ to $w_2$. On the other hand, there are no loops based at $w_2$ because there are no loops in the set $s^{-1}(w) \backslash L_w$. Moreover, the move (I-) introduces edges whose sources lie in the set
\begin{equation} \label{equation: I- Set}
\{ s(e) \; \vert \; e \in E^1, \; s(e) \neq w, \; r(e) = w \}
\end{equation}
and whose ranges are either $w_1$ or $w_2$.  \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now since $w_2$ does not support any loops, we may apply (CO) to it. The edges whose sources lie in the set given in \eqref{equation: I- Set} and whose ranges are $w_2$ induce a new set of edges whose sources lie in the same set and whose ranges are now $v$. Similarly, the $k$ edges from $w_1$ to $w_2$ induce new edges from $w_1$ to $v$. Hence, we obtain a graph such that the vertices in the set $$\{ s(e) \; \vert \; e \in E^1, \; s(e) \neq w, \; r(e) = w \} \cup \{ w_1 \}$$ all emit edges to $v$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
\textbf{Step 2:} We repeatedly apply step 1 to all edges $w \in E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ which emit edges to $v$, but receive edges from vertices which themselves do not emit an edge to $v$. The result is a graph where every vertex which emitted an edge to $w$ but previously did not emit an edge to $v$, now emits edges to $v$. The vertex $w$ is either deleted from the graph or replaced by a vertex which still emits edges to $v$. With each application of step 1, the number of vertices in the graph can only decrease. Since $E$ has finitely many vertices then this process must eventually terminate. We obtain a graph $F'$ where every vertex $w \in (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ emits at least one edge to $v$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
\textbf{Step 3: Ensuring every vertex emits exactly one edge to $v$.} \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Let $g$ denote the single loop based at $v$. If $w \in (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ then let
\begin{equation*}
E_{w}^1 = \{ e \in E^1 \; \vert \; \text{$s(e) = w$ and $r(e) = v$} \} 
\end{equation*}
and $h_w$ be an edge in $E_{w}^1$. Apply move (O) to $v$ with the following partition of $r^{-1}(v)$:
\begin{equation} \label{equation: QDS O Partition}
{\bigsqcup}_{w \in (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \}, \; \lvert E_w^1 \rvert > 1} \big(E_{w}^1 \backslash \{ h_w \} \big) \sqcup \big\{ g, h_w \; \vert \; w \in (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \} \big\}. 
\end{equation}
The idea behind this partition is that the set containing the single loop $g$ takes exactly one edge from all the sets $E_{w}^1$. Applying move (O) with this partition replaces $v$ with vertices $\{ x_1, x_2, \dots, x_r \} \sqcup \{ y \}$ such that for $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$, $x_i$ emits exactly one edge to $y$. The vertex $y$ receives exactly one edge from every vertex $w \in (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ and supports a single loop. So if $G$ is the resulting graph whose vertices are
\begin{equation*}
G^0 = \big( (F')^0 \backslash \{ v \} \big) \sqcup \{ x_1, \dots, x_r \} \sqcup \{ y \}
\end{equation*}
and $F$ is the subgraph of $G$ whose vertices are $G^0 \backslash \{ y \}$ then $G = S^2 F$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Refined Moves Stable Iso}, $C^*(E)$ and $C^*(S^2 F)$ are stably isomorphic. To see that $C^*(H)$ and $C^*(F)$ are also stably isomorphic, we track how the application of moves to $E$ in each step affects $H$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
In step 2, the repeated application of step 1 consists of moves which all happen within $H$. Let $H'$ be the finite graph obtained from $H$ after the application of such moves. The application of move (O) in step 3 produces extra vertices which emit exactly one edge to a vertex supporting a single loop. Within the subgraph $F$ of $S^2 F$, these new vertices are regular sinks. By applying move (S) to remove them, we recover the finite graph $H'$ from $F$. Thus by Proposition \ref{proposition: Refined Moves Stable Iso}, $C^*(F)$ is stably isomorphic to $C^*(H')$ and hence, stably isomorphic to $C^*(H)$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
To illustrate the steps in the proof of Proposition \ref{proposition: QDS Forcing}, suppose that $E$ is the graph
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (0, 0) {$x$};
\node (2) at (3, 0) {$w$};
\node (3) at (6, 0) {$v$};
\draw[->] (1) to [bend left = 20] (2);
\draw[->] (1) to [bend right = 20] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 225, in = 315, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to (3);
\draw[->] (3) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (3);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation*}
Applying move (I-) to the vertex $w$ with the partition in \eqref{equation: QDS I- Partition} produces the graph \vspace{-1 em}
\begin{equation} \label{equation: QDS Example 1}
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (0, 0) {$x$};
\node (2) at (3, 1) {$w_1$};
\node (4) at (3, -1) {$w_2$};
\node (3) at (6, 0) {$v$};
\draw[->] (1) to node[midway, above] {(2)} (2);
\draw[->] (1) to node[midway, below] {(2)} (4);
\draw[->] (2) to node[midway, right] {(2)} (4);
\draw[->] (4) to (3);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 15, in = 75, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 90, in = 150, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (3) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (3);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation}
In graph \ref{equation: QDS Example 1}, the numbers labelling the edges denote their multiplicities. Next, applying move (CO) to the vertex $w_2$ in graph \eqref{equation: QDS Example 1} produces the graph \vspace{-1 em}
\begin{equation} \label{equation: QDS Example 2}
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (0, -1) {$x$};
\node (2) at (0, 1) {$w_1$};
\node (3) at (3, 0) {$v$};
\draw[->] (1) to node[midway, left] {(2)} (2);
\draw[->] (1) to node[midway, below] {(2)} (3);
\draw[->] (2) to node[midway, above] {(2)} (3);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 15, in = 75, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 90, in = 150, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (3) to [out = 45, in = 135, looseness = 10] (3);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation}
Finally, applying move (O)  to the vertex $v$ in graph \ref{equation: QDS Example 2} with the partition in \eqref{equation: QDS O Partition} produces the following graph, which as promised by Proposition \ref{proposition: QDS Forcing}, is a quantum double suspension graph: \vspace{-1 em}
\begin{equation*} 
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current  bounding  box.center)] 
\node (1) at (0, -1) {$x$};
\node (2) at (0, 1) {$w_1$};
\node (3) at (4, -1) {$x_2$};
\node (4) at (4, 1) {$x_1$};
\node (5) at (6, 0) {$y$};
\draw[->] (1) to node[midway, left] {(2)} (2);
\draw[->] (2) to (4);
\draw[->] (1) to (3);
\draw[->] (1) to (5);
\draw[->] (2) to (5);
\draw[->] (3) to (5);
\draw[->] (4) to (5);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 15, in = 75, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (2) to [out = 90, in = 150, looseness = 10] (2);
\draw[->] (5) to [out = 315, in = 45, looseness = 10] (5);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
A \textbf{skeleton} is a pair $(S, c)$ where $S$ is a finite acyclic graph such that there exists at most one edge between any pair of distinct vertices in $S$ and $c$ is a function from $S^0$ to $\{0, 1, \infty \}$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{definition: Skeleton Graph}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Define an equivalence relation $\sim_E$ on $E^0$ by setting for $v, w \in E^0$, $v \sim_E w$ if and only if $v \geq w$ and $w \geq v$. That is, $v$ and $w$ both lie on the same cycle in $E$. The \textbf{skeleton} of $E$, denoted by $S(E)$, is a graph defined by the following data:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The vertices $S(E)^0$ are elements of the set $E^0/\sim_E$, which will be denoted by $\check{v}$ for $v \in E^0$. 
\item If $\check{v}, \check{w} \in S(E)^0$ are distinct then connect $\check{v}$ to $\check{w}$ by a single edge if and only if there exist $v', w' \in E^0$ and $e \in E^1$ such that $v \sim_E v'$, $w \sim_E w'$, $s(e) = v'$ and $r(e) = w'$ in the graph $E$. 
\end{enumerate}
The graph $S(E)$ is also accompanied by the function $c: S(E)^0 \rightarrow \{0, 1, \infty \}$ defined by
\begin{equation*}
c(\check{v}) = 
\begin{cases}
0, \text{ if $v \in E^0$ is a source,} \\
1, \text{ if $v \in E^0$ supports a single loop,} \\
\infty, \text{ if $v \in E^0$ supports more than one cycle.} 
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{definition: Gauge Length}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and $n > 0$. The graph C*-algebra $C^*(E)$ is said to have \textbf{gauge length} $n$ if there exists an ascending chain of gauge-invariant ideals
\begin{equation*}
I_0 = \{ 0 \} \subseteq I_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq I_{n-1} \subseteq I_n = C^*(E)
\end{equation*}
such that if $j \in \{0, 1, \dots, n-1 \}$ and $H_j$ is the hereditary subset corresponding to $I_j$ via \eqref{equation: Hereditary Saturated} then the quotient $C^*(H_{j+1} \backslash H_j)$ is gauge-simple.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Gauge Simple}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then $C^*(E)$ is gauge-simple (equivalently, has gauge length one) if and only if $\lvert S(E)^0 \rvert = 1$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First assume that $S(E)^0 = \{ \check{v} \}$. If $c(\check{v}) = 0$ then by standing assumptions \ref{property: S1} and \ref{property: S2}, $v$ is a source vertex in $E$. Moreover, $v$ is the unique vertex of $E$ and consequently, $C^*(E) \cong \mathbb{C}$ is simple. If $c(\check{v}) = 1$ then $v$ supports a single loop in $E$. Since $S(E)^0 = \{ \check{v} \}$ then $v$ is again the unique vertex in $E$ and so $C^*(E) \cong C(\mathbb{T})$ is gauge-simple. Finally, if $c(\check{v}) = \infty$ then $v$ supports multiple cycles in $E$ and thus, $E$ cannot consist of a single cycle. Since every vertex $w \in E^0$ satisfies $v \geq w$ and $w \geq v$ then by \cite[Proposition 4.2]{Rae05} and \cite[Remark 5.6]{BPRS00}, $C^*(E)$ is simple purely infinite. In all cases, we have that $C^*(E)$ is gauge-simple. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Conversely, assume that $\lvert S(E)^0 \rvert > 1$. Let $\check{v}, \check{w} \in S(E)^0$ be distinct. By definition of $S(E)$, either $\check{v} \not \geq \check{w}$ or $\check{w} \not \geq \check{v}$ in $E$. So either $L(v)$ or $L(w)$ is a proper hereditary subset of $E^0$. Hence, $C^*(E)$ is not gauge-simple.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Gauge Length}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then the gauge length of $C^*(E)$ is $\lvert S(E)^0 \rvert$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on the gauge length of $C^*(E)$. The base case where $C^*(E)$ has gauge length one is done by Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Simple}. Now suppose that the statement is true for graphs $E$ such that $C^*(E)$ has gauge length $n > 0$. Assume that $C^*(E)$ has gauge length $n + 1$. There exists an ascending chain of gauge-invariant ideals
\begin{equation*}
\{ 0 \} = I_0 \subseteq I_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq I_n \subseteq I_{n+1} = C^*(E)
\end{equation*}
and its associated ascending chain of hereditary subsets
\begin{equation*}
\emptyset = H_0 \subseteq H_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq H_n \subseteq H_{n+1} = E^0
\end{equation*}
such that if $j \in \{0, 1, \dots, n \}$ then $C^*(H_{j+1} \backslash H_j)$ is gauge-simple. Restricting to the subgraph $H_n$, we have the ascending chain of gauge-invariant ideals
\begin{equation*}
\{ 0 \} = I_0 \subseteq I_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq I_{n-1} \subseteq C^*(H_n).
\end{equation*}
So $C^*(H_n)$ has gauge length $n$ and by the inductive hypothesis, $\lvert S(H_n)^0 \rvert = n$. Now by assumption, the quotient $C^*(E \backslash H_n)$ is gauge-simple and subsequently $\lvert S(E \backslash H_n)^0 \rvert = 1$ by the base case. Therefore, 
\begin{equation*}
\lvert S(E)^0 \rvert = \lvert S(H_n)^0 \rvert +  \lvert S(E \backslash H_n)^0 \rvert = n + 1.
\end{equation*}
This completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $H$ be a hereditary subset of $S$. We say that a vertex $v \in H$ is \textbf{terminal} (or a terminal vertex for $H$) if for $w \in H$ satisfying $v \geq w$, $v = w$. The set of vertices in $H$ which are terminal is denoted by $H_t$.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}
Let $S$ be a skeleton and $H$ be a hereditary subset of $S$. For $v \in S^0$, let $L_S(v)$ be the hereditary subset $\{ x \in S^0 \; \vert \; x \geq v \}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
H = {\bigcup}_{v \in H_t} L_S(v). 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The inclusion $\bigcup_{v \in H_t} L_S(v)\subseteq H$ follows from the assumption that $H$ is hereditary. To see that the reverse inclusion holds, assume that $w \in H$. We claim that there exists $v \in H_t$ such that $w \geq v$. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $w$ does not admit a finite path to any terminal vertex for $H$. Then $w$ is not a terminal vertex for $H$ and so, there exists $w_1 \in H$ such that $w \geq w_1$ and $w_1 \not \geq w$. By our assumption on $w$, $w_1$ is also not terminal. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
By repeating this argument indefinitely, there exist vertices $w_1, w_2, \dots$ in $H$ which are not terminal vertices for $H$ such that
\begin{equation*}
w \geq w_1 \geq w_2 \geq w_3 \geq \dots
\end{equation*}
and $w_{i+1} \not \geq w_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$. In particular, the vertices $w, w_1, w_2, \dots$ are all pairwise distinct and hence, we have constructed a path of infinite length in $H$, contradicting the fact that $S$ has finitely many vertices. Thus, there exists a terminal vertex $x \in H$ such that 
\begin{equation*}
w \in L_S(x) \subseteq {\bigcup}_{v \in H_t} L_S(v). 
\end{equation*}
So $H \subseteq \bigcup_{v \in H_t} L_S(v)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{definition: Cu E}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton. Define $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ to be the set of functions $f: S_\kappa \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{N}}$ which satisfy the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $v \in S^0$ and $c(v) = 1$ then $f(v) \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. 
\item If $v \in S^0$ and $c(v) = \infty$ then $f(v) \in \{0, \infty \}$. 
\item If $v, w \in S^0$, $w \geq v$ and $f(v) \neq 0$ then $f(w) = \infty$. 
\end{enumerate}
In the special case where $(S, c)$ is the skeleton of a finite graph $E$ satisfying the standing assumptions, we denote $\operatorname{Cu}_{S(E)}$ more simply by $\operatorname{Cu}_E$.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Order Alternative}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. Then $f \leq g$ if and only if the following statements are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. 
\item Suppose that $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is a terminal vertex such that $c(w) \neq \infty$. Then $f(w) \leq g(w)$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The ``only if" direction follows from the fact that the order on $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ is pointwise. Conversely, assume that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfy the two properties in the statement of the lemma. Assume that $w \in S^0$. If $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is terminal and $c(w) \neq \infty$ then by the second assumption, $f(w) \leq g(w)$. Otherwise, $g(w) \in \{0, \infty \}$ and since $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ then $f(w) \leq g(w)$. Using the fact that the orders on $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ are both pointwise, $f \leq g$ pointwise.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Way Below}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. Then $f \ll g$ if and only if the following statements are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. 
\item Suppose that $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is a terminal vertex satisfying $c(w) \neq \infty$. Then $f(w) \ll g(w)$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Assume that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$ and $f \ll g$. Then $f \leq g$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. To see that the second property is satisfied, assume that $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is a terminal vertex satisfying $c(w) = 0$. Then $g(w) \in \overline{\mathbb{N}} \backslash \{ 0 \}$. Let $\{ n_k \}_{k > 0}$ be an increasing sequence in $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $n_1 \neq 0$ and $g(w) \leq \sup_{k > 0} n_k$. If $k \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ then the function
\begin{equation*}
h_k = n_k \cdot \chi_{\{ w \}} + (g - g(w)) 
\end{equation*}
defines an increasing sequence $\{ h_k \}_{k}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$. Let $h = \sup_{k > 0} h_k$ and $n = \sup_{k > 0} n_k$. Since the supremum in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ is given pointwise, $${\sup}_{k > 0} \; h_k = h = n \cdot \chi_{\{ w \}} + (g - g(w)) \geq g.$$ Now using that $f \ll g$, there exists $\ell \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ such that $f \leq h_\ell$. In particular, $f(w) \leq h_\ell(w) = n_\ell$. So $f(w) \ll g(w)$ in $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$. An analogous argument handles the case where $c(w) = 1$. This proves the ``only if" direction of the lemma. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Conversely, assume that the two properties in the statement of the lemma are satisfied. Let $\{ a_m \}_{m > 0}$ be an increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ with supremum $a$ and suppose that $a \geq g$. Then we have an ascending chain 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(a_1) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(a_2) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(a_3) \subseteq \dots
\end{equation*}
of hereditary subsets of $S^0$. Since $S$ has finitely many vertices then there are finitely many hereditary subsets of $S^0$. Hence, the ascending chain must terminate and there exists $m' \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ such that for $j \geq 0$, $$\operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(a) = \operatorname{supp}_0(a_{m' + j}) = \operatorname{supp}_0(a_{m'}).$$ Now assume that $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(a)$ is a terminal vertex such that $c(w) \neq \infty$. If $w \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ then $w \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and so for $\ell \geq m'$, $f(w) = 0 \leq a_\ell(w)$. Otherwise, if $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ then by the second assumption, $$f(w) \ll g(w) \leq a(w)$$ in $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ and there exists $\ell' \geq m'$ such that $f(w) \leq a_{\ell'}(w)$. Consequently, there exists $\ell \geq m'$ large enough such that if $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(a) = \operatorname{supp}_0(a_\ell)$ is terminal  and $c(w) \neq \infty$ then $f(w) \leq a_{\ell}(w)$. Since $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(a) = \operatorname{supp}_0(a_\ell)$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, $f \leq a_\ell$ and thus, $f \ll g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Axiom O3}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f, f', g, g' \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. If $f' \ll f$ and $g' \ll g$ then $f' + g' \ll f + g$. That is, $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O3}.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Assume that $f, f', g, g' \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$ are such that $f' \ll f$ and $g' \ll g$. Then $f' + g' \leq f + g$ pointwise and $\operatorname{supp}_0(f' + g') \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f + g)$. Next, assume that $x \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f + g) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f + g)$ such that $c(x) \neq \infty$. Then either $x\in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ is terminal or $x \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ is terminal. In either case, we have
\begin{equation*}
(f' + g')(x) = f'(x) + g'(x) \ll f(x) + g(x) = (f + g)(x).
\end{equation*}
Hence by Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below}, $f' + g' \ll f + g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{definition: Singletons}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $v \in S^0$ be such that $c(v) = 0$ and $n \in \overline{\mathbb{N}} \backslash \{ 0 \}$. Let $L_S(v) = \{ x \in S^0 \; \vert \; x \geq v \}$. Define 
\begin{equation*}
\theta_{v, n} = n \cdot \chi_{\{ v \}} + \infty \cdot \chi_{L_S(v)_\kappa \backslash \{ v \}}. 
\end{equation*}
Next suppose that $c(v) = \infty$. Define $\theta_{v, \infty} = \infty \cdot \chi_{L_S(v)_\kappa}$. Finally, suppose that $c(v) = 1$ and $f \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \backslash \{ 0 \}$. Define 
\begin{equation*}
\theta_{v, f} = f \vert_{\mathbb{T}_{v}} + \infty \cdot \chi_{L_S(v)_\kappa \backslash \mathbb{T}_{v}}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Singleton Decomp}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. Then
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Singleton Decomp}
f = {\sum}_{v \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} \theta_{v, f(v)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Definition \ref{definition: Singletons},  the RHS of \eqref{equation: Singleton Decomp} is an element of $\operatorname{Cu}_S$, which we denote by $g$. By construction of $g$ and Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal},
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(g) = {\bigcup}_{v\in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} L_S(v) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f).
\end{equation*}
Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Axiom O2}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. There exists a rapidly increasing sequence $\{ f_n \}_{n > 0}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ such that $\sup_{n > 0} f_n = f$. That is, $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O2}.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Assume that $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp},
\begin{equation*} 
f = {\sum}_{v \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} \theta_{v, f(v)}.
\end{equation*}
If $v \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ and $c(v) = 0$ then $f(v) \neq 0$ in $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ and there exists a rapidly increasing sequence $\{ n_{v, k} \}_{k > 0}$ such that $n_{v, 1} \neq 0$ and $\sup_{k > 0} n_{v, k} = f(v)$. Hence the sequence $\{ \theta_{v, n_{v, k}} \}_{k > 0}$ is a rapidly increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfying ${\sup}_{k > 0} \; \theta_{v, n_{v, k}}  =  \theta_{v, f(v)}$. If $c(v) = 1$ then the same argument shows that we can produce a rapidly increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ with supremum $\theta_{v, f(v)}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Axiom O3}, we obtain a rapidly increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ with supremum $f$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton. Then $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ is a Cu-semigroup. In particular, if $E$ is a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions then $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is a Cu-semigroup.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Recall that $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O1} because the supremum of an increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ is simply given by the pointwise supremum. It follows directly from this that $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O4}. Finally, by Lemma \ref{lemma: Axiom O2} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Axiom O3}, $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O2} and \ref{axiom: O3}. So $\operatorname{Cu}_S$ is a Cu-semigroup.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Maximal Tail Is Terminal}
Let $J$ be an ideal of $C^*(E)$ as in \eqref{equation: Non Gauge Invariant Form}. If $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ then $\check{v}_j \in S(E)^0$ is a terminal vertex for the hereditary subset $\langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$ of $S(E)^0$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
In the degenerate case where $n = 0$, there is nothing to show. So assume that $n \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ and that $J$ satisfies properties \ref{property: I1}, \ref{property: I2} and \ref{property: I3}. If $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ then $\check{v}_j \in \langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$. To see that $\check{v}_j$ is terminal for $\langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$, let $\check{w} \in \langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$ and assume that $\check{v}_j \geq \check{w}$. Then $v_j \geq w$ in $E$. Now since $v_j \not \in H \cap \bigcap_{i = 1}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i))$ then $w \not \in H \cap \bigcap_{i = 1}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i))$ because the set $H \cap \bigcap_{i = 1}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i))$ is hereditary. Since $w \in \mathcal{D}_J$ then by \eqref{equation: Hereditary DJ}, there exists $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ such that $w = v_k$. By property \ref{property: I3}, $$w = v_k \in H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1, \; i \neq k}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i))$$ and since the above set is hereditary, it must also contain $v_j$. Consequently, $j = k$, $v_j = v_k = w$ and $\check{v}_j$ is a terminal vertex for $\langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Non Gauge Invariant Ideal}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
I = I_H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i} \qquad \text{and} \qquad J = I_{H'} \cap {\bigcap}_{j = 1}^q \mathcal{R}_{w_j, L_j}
\end{equation*}
be ideals of $C^*(E)$. Suppose that as ideals of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$, $\mathcal{I}(I) = \mathcal{I}(J)$. Then $I = J$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
First, assume that $n = q = 0$ so that $I = I_H$ and $J = I_{H'}$ are both gauge-invariant ideals of $C^*(E)$. Since $\mathcal{I}(I) = \mathcal{I}(J)$ then by \eqref{equation: Ideal Lattice 1} and \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton}, $\langle H \rangle = \langle H' \rangle$ and $I = I_H = I_{H'} = J$. Now assume that $n, q \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ so that $I$ and $J$ are non-gauge-invariant. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Maximal Tail Is Terminal}, $\{ \check{v}_1, \dots, \check{v}_n \} \subseteq \langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle_t$. Using this, we define 
\begin{equation*}
g = {\sum}_{\check{x} \in \langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle_t \backslash \{ \check{v}_1, \dots, \check{v}_n \}} \; \theta_{\check{x}, \delta_{\check{x}}}  + {\sum}_{i = 1}^n \theta_{\check{v}_i, \; \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash K_i}}. 
\end{equation*}
By Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(g) = {\bigcup}_{\check{x} \in \langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle_t} L_{S(E)}(\check{x}) = \langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle.
\end{equation*}
Consequently, $g \in \mathcal{I}(I)$ and $\langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle = \operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$. By interchanging the roles of $H$ and $H'$ and the roles of $\{ v_1, \dots, v_n \}$ and $\{ w_1, \dots, w_q \}$, $\langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle = \langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next we claim that $\{ v_1, \dots, v_n \} = \{w_1, \dots, w_q \}$. Assume that $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ and suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is no $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, q \}$ such that $v_k \neq w_j$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Maximal Tail Is Terminal}, $\check{v}_i \in S(E)^0$ is a terminal vertex for $\langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle = \langle \mathcal{D}_J \rangle$. Since $v_i \neq w_j$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, q \}$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, $$\theta_{\check{v}_i, \; \chi_{\mathbb{T}}} \in \mathcal{I}(J) = \mathcal{I}(I).$$ Hence, $\operatorname{supp}(\theta_{\check{v}_i, \; \chi_{\mathbb{T}}}(\check{v}_i)) = \mathbb{T} \subseteq \mathbb{T} \backslash K_i$. This contradicts the fact that by property \ref{property: I2}, $K_i$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{T}$. Hence, there exists $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, q \}$ such that $v_i = w_j$ and by a symmetric argument, $\{ v_1, \dots, v_n \} = \{ w_1, \dots, w_q \}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now since $\mathcal{D}_I = \mathcal{D}_J$ as hereditary subsets of $E^0$ then 
\begin{equation*}
H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) = H' \cap {\bigcap}_{j = 1}^q (E^0 \backslash R(w_j))
\end{equation*}
and by relabelling, we may assume that $v_i = w_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$. Now if $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ then
\begin{equation*}
\theta_{\check{v}_i, \; \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash K_i}} \in \left\{ f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \; \Big\vert \; 
\begin{matrix}
\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \langle \mathcal{D}_I \rangle \text{ and for $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$,} \\
\operatorname{supp}(f(\check{v}_i)) \subseteq \mathbb{T} \backslash L_i
\end{matrix}  \right\}
\end{equation*}
and subsequently, $K_i \subseteq L_i$. By interchanging the roles of $K_i$ and $L_i$, we have $K_i = L_i$. Finally by \eqref{equation: Sandwich}, 
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
I & = & I_H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i}
\\
& = & I_H \cap \Big({\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n I_{(E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) \sqcup \{ v_i \}} \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i}\Big)
\\
& = & I_{H \cap \bigcap_{i = 1}^n ((E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) \sqcup \{ v_i \})} \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i}.
\end{IEEEeqnarray*}
Using property \ref{property: I3},
\begin{equation*}
H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \big((E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) \sqcup \{ v_i \} \big) = \Big( H \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n (E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) \Big) \sqcup \{ v_1, \dots, v_n \} = \mathcal{D}_I
\end{equation*}
and combining this with the equality $\mathcal{D}_I = \mathcal{D}_J$, we find that
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
I & = & I_{H \cap \bigcap_{i = 1}^n ((E^0 \backslash R(v_i)) \sqcup \{ v_i \})} \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i}
\\
& = & I_{\mathcal{D}_I} \cap {\bigcap}_{i = 1}^n \mathcal{R}_{v_i, K_i}
\\
& = & I_{\mathcal{D}_J} \cap {\bigcap}_{j = 1}^q \mathcal{R}_{w_j, L_j}
\\
& = & I_{H' \cap \bigcap_{j = 1}^q ((E^0 \backslash R(w_j)) \sqcup \{ w_j \} )} \cap {\bigcap}_{j = 1}^q \mathcal{R}_{w_j, L_j} = J.
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Largest GII Below}
Let $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. As subsets of $E^0$, 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \backslash \{ w \in E^0 \; \vert \; \check{w} \in f_\partial \} = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial} (E^0 \backslash R(w)). 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
First, assume that $x \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial} (E^0 \backslash R(w))$. Since $x \in R(x)$ then $\check{x} \not \in f_\partial$ and
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial} (E^0 \backslash R(w)) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \backslash \{ w \in E^0 \; \vert \; \check{w} \in f_\partial \}. 
\end{equation*}
To see that the reverse inclusion holds, assume that $$x \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial} (E^0 \backslash R(w)).$$ Then either $x \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ or there exists $w \in E^0$ such that $\check{w} \in f_\partial$ and $x \in R(w)$. Observe that if $x \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ then there exists $y \in E^0$ such that $x \geq y$ and $\check{y} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. Since $x \in R(w)$ then $\check{w} \geq \check{x} \geq \check{y}$ in $S(E)$. But by definition of $f_\partial$, $\check{w}$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. So $\check{w} = \check{y}$ and $\check{x} = \check{w} \in f_\partial$. Consequently, we have proved that either $x \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ or $x \in \{ w \in E^0 \; \vert \; \check{w} \in f_\partial \}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theorem: Ideal Lattice Iso}
The map $\mathcal{I}: \operatorname{Lat}(C^*(E)) \rightarrow \operatorname{Lat}(\operatorname{Cu}_E)$ defined by \eqref{equation: Ideal Lattice 2} is bijective.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lemma: Non Gauge Invariant Ideal}, $\mathcal{I}$ is injective. To see that $\mathcal{I}$ is surjective, assume that $S$ is an ideal of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. First, observe that $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is a countably based Cu-semigroup (see Definition \ref{definition: Countably Based}). Indeed, if $\check{v} \in S(E)^0$ is such that $c(\check{v}) \neq \infty$ then we can use countable sup-dense subsets of $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ to write the function $\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}$ as the supremum of a rapidly increasing sequence of functions formed from these sup-dense subsets. The claim that $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is countably based then follows from Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp} and \ref{axiom: O4}. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now by \cite[Proposition 5.1.7]{APT18}, there exists $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $S = \operatorname{Idl}(f)$. If $f_\partial = \emptyset$ then by \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton} and \eqref{equation: Ideal Lattice 1}, 
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}(I_{\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger}) = \big\{ g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \; \vert \; \operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \big\} = \operatorname{Idl}(f). 
\end{equation*}
If $f_\partial \neq \emptyset$ then define the non-gauge-invariant ideal
\begin{equation*}
I_f = I_{\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger} \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{v} \in f_\partial} \mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash \operatorname{supp}(f(\check{v}))}. 
\end{equation*}
Since $f_\partial$ was assumed to be non-empty, $I_f$ satisfies property \ref{property: I2}. By definition, $I_f$ automatically satisfies property \ref{property: I1}. To see that $I_f$ satisfies property \ref{property: I3}, we need to show that if $v \in E^0$ is such that $\check{v} \in f_\partial$ then 
\begin{equation*}
v \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial, \; w \neq v } (E^0 \backslash R(w)). 
\end{equation*}
By definition of $f_\partial$, $v \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^{\dagger}$. Furthermore, if $w \in E^0$ is such that $\check{w} \in f_{\partial}$ and $v \in R(w)$ then $\check{w} \geq \check{v}$ and $\check{w} = \check{v}$ in $S(E)$ because $\check{w}$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. Since $w$ supports a single loop, we in fact have $v = w$ in $E$. So by the contrapositive, if $w \neq v$ then $v \in E^0 \backslash R(w)$. Consequently, $I_f$ satisfies property \ref{property: I3}.\newline
\phantom{} \newline
Recalling the definition of $\mathcal{D}_{I_f}$ from \eqref{equation: Hereditary DJ}, we have by Lemma \ref{lemma: Largest GII Below} that 
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{D}_{I_f} = \Big( \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \cap {\bigcap}_{\check{w} \in f_\partial} (E^0 \backslash R(w)) \Big) \sqcup \{ \check{w} \in E^0 \; \vert \; w \in f_\partial \} = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger. 
\end{equation*}
So by \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton} and \eqref{equation: Ideal Lattice 2}, $\langle \mathcal{D}_{I_f} \rangle = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ as hereditary subsets of $S(E)^0$ and
{ \small \begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}(I_f) = 
\left\{ g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \; \Big\vert \; 
\begin{matrix}
\operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \text{ and for $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$,} \\
\operatorname{supp}(g(\check{v}_i)) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(f(\check{v}_i))
\end{matrix}
\right\} = \operatorname{Idl}(f).
\end{equation*}}
Hence, $\mathcal{I}: \operatorname{Lat}(C^*(E)) \rightarrow \operatorname{Lat}(\operatorname{Cu}_E)$ is bijective.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{remark: POM Iso Between Cu Semigroups}
Let $S$ and $T$ be Cu-semigroups and $\phi: S \rightarrow T$ be an isomorphism of positively ordered monoids. Since suprema of increasing sequences and the way-below relation are defined in terms of the order, $\phi$ automatically preserves both way-below and suprema of increasing sequences. So $\phi$ is a Cu-isomorphism. This observation was noted in the remark at the end of the proof of \cite[Lemma 7.1.12]{APT18}, and justifies why $i_H$ is a Cu-isomorphism.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Cu E Minus H}
There exists a surjective Cu-morphism $\rho_H: \operatorname{Cu}_E \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ such that $$\ker \rho_H = \big\{ f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \; \vert \; \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \langle H \rangle \big\} \cong \operatorname{Cu}_H.$$
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Assume that $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp}, 
\begin{equation*}
f = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}. 
\end{equation*}
Recall the definition of $\langle E \backslash H \rangle$ from \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton}. Define $\rho_H(f)$ by
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Quotient}
\rho_H(f) = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in (\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}. 
\end{equation}
By construction, $\rho_H(f) \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$. To see that $\rho_H$ is additive, assume that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal},
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0(\rho_H(f + g)) = (\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(g)) \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle = \operatorname{supp}_0(\rho_H(f) + \rho_H(g)).
\end{equation*}
Now suppose that $\check{v} \in ((\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(g)) \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle)_t$ and $c(\check{v}) \neq \infty$. Observe that if $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle$ then by definition of a terminal vertex, $\check{v} \in (\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle)_t$. The same statement holds when $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ is replaced with $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. In the resulting three cases, we have by \eqref{equation: Quotient} that
\begin{equation*}
\rho_H(f + g)(\check{v}) = f(\check{v}) + g(\check{v}) = \rho_H(f)(\check{v}) + \rho_H(g)(\check{v}).
\end{equation*}
So by Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, $\rho_H(f + g) = \rho_H(f) + \rho_H(g)$. Using Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} once more, it is straightforward to check that $\rho_H$ is order preserving. The map $\rho_H$ is surjective because if $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ then 
\begin{equation*}
\rho_H \Big( {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, g(\check{v})} \Big) = g. 
\end{equation*}
Moreover, $\ker \rho_H$ is the set of all functions in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ with vertex support contained in $\langle H \rangle$ because $\langle H \rangle \cap \langle E \backslash H \rangle = \emptyset$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
It remains to show that $\rho_H$ is a Cu-morphism. The claim that $\rho_H$ is way-below preserving is proved in a similar fashion to showing that $\rho_H$ is order preserving, using Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below} in lieu of Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}. To see that $\rho_H$ preserves suprema of increasing sequences, let $\{ f_n \}_{n > 0}$ be an increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ with supremum $f$. Since $\rho_H$ is order preserving, $\{ \rho_H(f_n) \}_{n > 0}$ is an increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
We claim that $\rho_H(f) = \sup_{n > 0} \rho_H(f_n)$. To this end, assume that $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ is such that if $n \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ then $\rho_H(f_n) \leq g$. By viewing $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ as a subset of $S(E)^0$, we define $g'$ be the function
\begin{equation*}
g' = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, g(\check{v})} + \infty \cdot {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \langle H \rangle_t} \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}} \in \operatorname{Cu}_E.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} and \eqref{equation: Quotient}, $f_n \leq g'$ for $n \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ and $\rho_H(g') = g$. So $f \leq g'$ and $\rho_H(f) \leq \rho_H(g') = g$. Hence, $\rho_H$ preserves suprema of increasing sequences, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{proposition: First Iso Thm Cu E}
The Cu-semigroups $\operatorname{Cu}_E / \operatorname{Cu}_H$ and $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ are isomorphic.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
By Remark \ref{remark: POM Iso Between Cu Semigroups}, it suffices to show that $\operatorname{Cu}_E / \operatorname{Cu}_H$ and $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ are isomorphic as positively ordered monoids. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Cu E Minus H}, $\rho_H: \operatorname{Cu}_E \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$ is a surjective Cu-morphism with $\ker \rho_H = \operatorname{Cu}_H$. Define $\widetilde{\rho_H}$ to be the map
\begin{equation*}
\begin{matrix}
\widetilde{\rho_H}: & \operatorname{Cu}_E/\operatorname{Cu}_H & \rightarrow & \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H} \\
& [f]_{\operatorname{Cu}_H} & \mapsto & \rho_H(f). 
\end{matrix}
\end{equation*}
The map $\widetilde{\rho_H}$ is well-defined because $\ker \rho_H = \operatorname{Cu}_H$. It is also additive and order preserving because $\rho_H$ is. Now to see that $\widetilde{\rho_H}$ is an order-embedding, assume that $[f]_{\operatorname{Cu}_H}, [g]_{\operatorname{Cu}_H} \in \operatorname{Cu}_E / \operatorname{Cu}_H$ are such that $\rho_H(f) \leq \rho_H(g)$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$. Define
\begin{equation*}
g' = g + \infty \cdot {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \langle H \rangle_t} \theta_{\check{v}, \delta_{\check{v}}}. 
\end{equation*}
By combining Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} with the inequality $\rho_H(f) \leq \rho_H(g)$, $f \leq g'$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. Recalling the partial order on $\operatorname{Cu}_E/\operatorname{Cu}_H$ from Definition \ref{definition: Quotient Cu Semigroup}, we have that $[f]_{\operatorname{Cu}_H} \leq [g]_{\operatorname{Cu}_H}$ and thus, $\widetilde{\rho_H}$ is an order-embedding.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
