<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{definition: Cuntz Stack}
Let $(S, \leq_S, +_S)$ and $(T, \leq_T, +_T)$ be Cu-semigroups and suppose that $S$ has largest element $\infty_S$. The \textbf{stack} of $S$ below $T$, denoted by $S  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  T$, is the Cu-semigroup defined by the following data:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The underlying set is the disjoint union $S \sqcup (T \backslash \{ 0_T \})$ where $0_T$ is the zero element of $T$. 
\item Let $s_1, s_2 \in S$ and $t_1, t_2 \in T \backslash \{ 0_T \}$. The order on $S  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  T$ is given by $s_1 \leq s_2$ if and only if $s_1 \leq_S s_2$, $t_1 \leq t_2$ if and only if $t_1 \leq_T t_2$ and $s_1 \leq t_1$. 
\item Let $s_1, s_2 \in S$ and $t_1, t_2 \in T \backslash \{ 0_T \}$. Addition on $S  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  T$ is given by $s_1 + s_2 = s_1 +_S s_2$, $t_1 + t_2 = t_1 +_T t_2$ and $s_1 + t_1 = t_1$. 
\item The way-below relation of $S  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  T$ behaves similarly to the order.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Stack Characterisation}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*} 
be an extension of C*-algebras. Suppose that $I$ is separable so that $\operatorname{Cu}(I)$ has largest element $\infty_I$. Then $\operatorname{Cu}(A) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I)  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(B)$ if and only if for $x \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$, $x + \infty_I = x$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The ``only if" direction follows from Definition \ref{definition: Cuntz Stack}. Assume that $x \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and let $\pi: A \rightarrow B$ be the quotient map. Observe that if $y \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(y) \leq \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(x)$ then by Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS}, $y \leq x + \infty_I = x$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$. Hence, any element of $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$ lifts uniquely to an element of $\operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and the map $\phi: \operatorname{Cu}(A) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}(I)  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(B)$ defined by
\begin{equation*}
\phi(x) = 
\begin{cases}
x, \text{ viewed as an element of $\operatorname{Cu}(I)$ if $x \leq \infty_I$,} \\
\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(x), \text{ viewed as an element of $\operatorname{Cu}(B)$ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
is an isomorphism of positively ordered monoids and thus, a Cu-isomorphism by Remark \ref{remark: POM Iso Between Cu Semigroups}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{remark: Purely Large Absorption}
By Corollary \ref{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised}, if the Cuntz semigroup of an extension decomposes as the stack, then the extension must be purely large. However, Cuntz semigroups of C*-algebras which are purely large extensions do not always decompose as the stack of the Cuntz semigroup of the ideal below the Cuntz semigroup of the quotient. To illustrate this point, let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space. The C*-algebra $B(H)$ is a purely large extension of the Calkin algebra $Q(H)$ by $K(H)$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: Kucerovsky Ng}. Moreover by \cite[Theorem 6.4]{ABP11}, $$\operatorname{Cu}(B(H)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(K(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(Q(H)) \cong \overline{\mathbb{N}}  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \{0, \infty \}.$$ Now let $\tilde{K}$ denote the minimal unitisation of $K(H)$, which is a purely large extension of $\mathbb{C}$ by $K$. However, $$\operatorname{Cu}(\tilde{K}) \not \cong \overline{\mathbb{N}}  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \overline{\mathbb{N}}.$$ To see this, note that $\tilde{K}$ has stable rank one and thus, $\operatorname{Cu}(\tilde{K})$ is weakly cancellative by \cite[Theorem 4.3]{RW10}. On the other hand, by Definition \ref{definition: Cuntz Stack}, $\overline{\mathbb{N}}  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \overline{\mathbb{N}}$ is not weakly cancellative.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Purely Large Axiom (O5)}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, "\pi"] & B \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be a purely large extension such that $I$ is separable and $B$ is stably finite. Let $\infty_I$ be the largest element in $\operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and $z \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$. Either $z + \infty_I = z$ or there exists a projection $p \in B \otimes K$ such that $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(z) = [p]$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Assume that $x \in (A \otimes K)_+ \backslash (I \otimes K)$ and $\epsilon > 0$. Then
\begin{equation*}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] \ll \Big[ \Big(x - \frac{\epsilon}{2} \Big)_+ \Big] \ll [x]. 
\end{equation*}
Applying (O5), there exists $y_\epsilon \in \operatorname{Cu}(A)$ such that 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Axiom (O5) Application}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] + y_\epsilon  \leq [x] \leq \Big[ \Big(x - \frac{\epsilon}{2} \Big)_+ \Big] + y_\epsilon. 
\end{equation}
Firstly, if there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that $y_\epsilon \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ then by the RHS inequality of \eqref{equation: Axiom (O5) Application},
\begin{equation*}
[\pi(x)] \leq \Big[ \Big(\pi(x) - \frac{\epsilon}{2} \Big)_+ \Big] \ll [\pi(x)]. 
\end{equation*}
So $[\pi(x)] \in \operatorname{Cu}(B)$ is compact. Since $B$ is stably finite then by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{BC09}, there exists a projection $p \in (B \otimes K)_+$ such that $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([x]) = [\pi(x)] = [p]$. On the other hand, suppose that for $\epsilon > 0$, $y_\epsilon \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$. By the LHS inequality of \eqref{equation: Axiom (O5) Application} and Corollary \ref{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised},
\begin{equation*}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] + \infty_I \leq [(x - \epsilon)_+] + y_\epsilon \leq [x]. 
\end{equation*}
Taking the supremum over all $\epsilon > 0$, we have $[x] + \infty_I = [x]$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Not Ideal Properly Infinite}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r] & 0 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be a purely large extension of C*-algebras. Suppose that $B$ is purely infinite. If $z \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ then $2z = z$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Assume that $A$ is a purely large extension of $B$ by $I$ and that $B$ is purely infinite. Assume that $[x] \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$. To show that $x$ is properly infinite, it suffices by \cite[Proposition 3.3 (iii)]{KR00} to show that if $\epsilon > 0$ then there exist mutually orthogonal positive elements $a_1, a_2 \in \overline{x (A \otimes K) x}$ such that for $j \in \{1, 2 \}$, $(x - \epsilon)_+ \precsim a_j$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Assume that $\epsilon > 0$ is small enough so that $(x - \epsilon)_+ \not \in (I \otimes K)_+$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: Purely Infinite Properly Infinite} and Lemma \ref{lemma: KR Lemma}, there exist mutually orthogonal positive elements $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4 \in \overline{x (A \otimes K) x}$ and a positive element $c \in \overline{x (I \otimes K) x}$ such that $a_1, a_2, a_3$ and $a_4$ are Cuntz equivalent to each other and for $j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4 \}$, 
\begin{equation*}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] \leq [a_j \oplus c] = [a_j] + [c]. 
\end{equation*}
Now observe that if $j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4 \}$ then $[a_j] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ because $[(x - \epsilon)_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and $[c] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$. Since $a_j$ and $c$ are positive elements of $A \otimes K$ then by Corollary \ref{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised}, 
\begin{equation*}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] \leq [a_1] + [c] \leq [a_1] + [a_2] = [a_1 + a_2].
\end{equation*}
Similarly, $[(x - \epsilon)_+] \leq [a_3 + a_4]$. So $a_1 + a_2$ and $a_3 + a_4$ are mutually orthogonal positive elements in $\overline{x (A \otimes K) x}$ which Cuntz dominate $(x - \epsilon)_+$ and hence, $(x - \delta)_+$ for $\delta \geq \epsilon$. If $\mu < \epsilon$ then $[(x - \mu)_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I)$ and we may repeat the above argument with $\mu$ in place of $\epsilon$ to obtain two mutually orthogonal positive elements in $\overline{x (A \otimes K) x}$ which Cuntz dominate $(x - \mu)_+$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{theorem: Purely Large Purely Infinite Quotient}
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r] & 0 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be a purely large extension of C*-algebras. Suppose that $I$ is separable and $B$ is purely infinite. Then $$\operatorname{Cu}(A) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I)  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(B).$$
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Assume that $x \in \operatorname{Cu}(A) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I)$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Not Ideal Properly Infinite}, we have that $2x = x$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$. Thus, if $\infty_I$ is the largest element of $\operatorname{Cu}(I)$ then by Corollary \ref{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised}, $x + \infty_I \leq 2x = x$. So $x + \infty_I = x$ and we are done by Proposition \ref{proposition: Stack Characterisation}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Assume that $v \in E^0$ is as in Theorem \ref{introtheorem: General Cuntz Krieger} and supports multiple cycles. It is easy to check that $H$ is hereditary and saturated. By \cite[Theorem 4.1]{BPRS00}, we have the extension
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Typical Graph Extension}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I_H  \arrow[r] & C^*(E) \arrow[r] & C^*(E \backslash H) \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Since every vertex in $E^0$ admits a path to $v$, 
\begin{equation*}
(E \backslash H)^0 = E^0 \backslash H = \{ x \in E^0 \; \vert \; \text{$x \geq v$ and $v \geq x$} \}. 
\end{equation*}
By assumption, $v \in E^0 \backslash H$ supports more than one cycle. So $E \backslash H$ cannot consist of just a single cycle. Subsequently by \cite[Proposition 4.2]{Rae05} and \cite[Remark 5.6]{BPRS00}, $C^*(E \backslash H)$ is simple purely infinite.  \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now since $C^*(E)$ is a unital extension with a simple quotient, it is full. To see that it is purely large, first note that by \cite[Lemma 1.6]{DHS03}, there exists a row-finite graph $E_H$ such that $I_H \cong C^*(E_H)$. By \cite[Theorem 3.2]{Tom04} and the structure of $E_H$, $I_H \cong C^*(E_H)$ is stable. So by \eqref{equation: Full Corner Iso}, $I_H \cong C^*(H) \otimes K$ and thus, $I_H$ is $\sigma$-unital and has the corona factorisation property by Proposition \ref{proposition: Graph CFP}. By Theorem \ref{theorem: Kucerovsky Ng}, $C^*(E)$ is a purely large extension. Theorem \ref{theorem: Purely Large Purely Infinite Quotient} finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Purely Large Circle Quotient}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and suppose that there exists $v \in E^0$ such that $v$ supports a single loop $g$ and if $w \in E^0$ then $w \geq v$. Let $H = \{ x \in E^0 \; \vert \; v \not \geq x \} = E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$. Then $C^*(E)$ is a purely large extension of $C(\mathbb{T})$ by $I_H \cong C^*(H) \otimes K$ if and only if $$\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}).$$
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Positive I Arbitrarily Small}
Let $y \in (I_H)_+$ and $\epsilon > 0$. Then there exists $k \geq 0$ such that $\lVert (s_g^*)^k y s_g^k \rVert \leq \epsilon$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By density, there exists a positive element
\begin{equation*}
y' \in \operatorname{span} \big\{ s_\mu s_\nu^* \; \vert \; \mu, \nu \in E^*, \; s(\mu) = s(\nu) \in H \big\}
\end{equation*}
such that $\lVert y - y' \rVert < \epsilon$. By the Cuntz-Krieger relations for $E$, there exists $k \geq 0$ large enough such that $(s_g^*)^k y' s_g^k = 0$. So
\begin{equation*}
\big\lVert (s_g^*)^k y s_g^k \big\rVert = \big\Vert (s_g^*)^k y s_g^k - (s_g^*)^k y' s_g^k \big\rVert \leq \lVert s_g^k \rVert^2 \lVert y - y' \rVert < \epsilon. \qedhere
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Sg Cutdown}
Let $x \in \operatorname{span} \{ s_\mu s_\nu^* \; \vert \; \mu, \nu \in E^*, \; s(\mu) = s(\nu) = v \}$. Then there exists $k \geq 0$ such that $(s_g^*)^k x s_g^k = c_x(s_g)$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let 
\begin{equation*}
x = {\sum}_{i = 1}^n \lambda_i s_{\mu_i} s_{\nu_i}^* \in \operatorname{span} \big\{ s_\mu s_\nu^* \; \big\vert \; \mu, \nu \in E^*, \; s(\mu) = s(\nu) = v \big\}. 
\end{equation*}
If $k = \max \{ \ell(\mu_i), \ell(\nu_i) \; \vert \; i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \} \}$ then by \eqref{equation: Paths In W Cutdown}, 
\begin{equation*}
(s_g^*)^k x s_g^k \in \operatorname{span} \big\{ p_v, s_g^m, (s_g^*)^n \; \big\vert \; m, n > 0 \big\}. 
\end{equation*}
Moreover by \eqref{equation: Quotient Form},
\begin{equation*}
\pi \big((s_g^*)^k x s_g^k \big) = (\pi(s_g)^*)^k \pi(x) \pi(s_g)^k = \pi(x) = c_x(\pi(s_g)) = \pi(c_x(s_g)). 
\end{equation*}
So there exists $i \in I_H$ such that $(s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g) = i$. Now if $\epsilon > 0$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Positive I Arbitrarily Small}, there exists $p \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ such that $\lVert (s_g^*)^p i s_g^p \rVert < \epsilon$. Since $$(s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g)  \in \operatorname{span} \{ p_v, s_g^m, (s_g^*)^n \; \vert \; m, n > 0 \}$$ then by \eqref{equation: Paths In W Cutdown},
\begin{equation*}
(s_g^*)^p \big( (s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g) \big) s_g^p = (s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g)
\end{equation*}
and $\lVert (s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g) \rVert = \lVert (s_g^*)^p i s_g^p \rVert < \epsilon$. Since $\epsilon > 0$ was arbitrary then $(s_g^*)^k x s_g^k - c_x(s_g) = 0$ as required.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Span Matrix Cutdown Quotients To Projection}
Let $n \geq 1$ and $x = (x_{ij})_{i, j = 1}^n \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+$ be such that $x_{ij} \in \mathcal{L}(E)$ for $i, j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$. Let $m > 0$ and suppose that $[\pi((x - \frac{1}{m})_+)] = n \cdot [\pi(p_v)]$. Then $$\Big[ \Big(x - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] = n \cdot [p_v]$$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ and $[(x - \frac{1}{m})_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [(x - \frac{1}{m})_+]$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Let $1_n \in C(\mathbb{T}) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ be the identity matrix. Since the entries of $x$ lie in $\mathcal{L}(E)$, we have $\pi(x) = \big(c_{x_{ij}}(\pi(s_g)) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n$ by \eqref{equation: Quotient Form}. Diagonalising the matrix $(c_{x_{ij}})_{i, j = 1}^n \in M_n(C(\mathbb{T}))_+$ pointwise, we see that if $z \in \mathbb{T}$ then there exist a unitary $u_z \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_1(z), \lambda_2(z), \dots, \lambda_n(z) \geq 0$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\big(c_{x_{ij}}(z) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n = u_z^* 
\begin{pmatrix}
\lambda_1(z) & & & \\
& \lambda_2(z) & & \\
& & \ddots & \\
& & & \lambda_n(z)
\end{pmatrix} u_z. 
\end{equation*}
If we cut down the positive matrix $\big(c_{x_{ij}}(z) \big)_{i, j}$ by $\frac{1}{m}$, the resulting matrix still has full rank because $[(\pi(x) - \frac{1}{m})_+] = n \cdot [\pi(p_v)]$. So, if $z \in \mathbb{T}$ and $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n \}$ then $\lambda_i(z) > \frac{1}{m}$ and consequently, there exists $\mu > 0$ small enough such that for $z \in \mathbb{T}$,
\begin{equation*}
\big(c_{x_{ij}}(z) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n \geq u_z^* \Big(\Big(\mu + \frac{1}{m} \Big) 1_n(z) \Big) u_z = \Big(\mu + \frac{1}{m} \Big) 1_n(z). 
\end{equation*}
Since $z \in \mathbb{T}$ was arbitrary then as positive elements in $M_n(C(\mathbb{T}))$,
\begin{equation*}
\pi(x) = \big(c_{x_{ij}}(\pi(s_g)) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n \geq \Big(\mu + \frac{1}{m} \Big) \cdot (\pi(p_v) \otimes 1_n).
\end{equation*}
Since $\pi(x) = \pi \big( (c_{x_{ij}}(s_g))_{i, j} \big)$ then there exist $y \in M_n(C^*(E))$ and $i \in I_H \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ self-adjoint such that 
\begin{equation*}
\big(c_{x_{ij}}(s_g) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n - \Big(\mu + \frac{1}{m} \Big) \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) = y^* y + i. 
\end{equation*}
Now write $i = i_+ - i_-$ where $i_+$ and $i_-$ are the positive and negative parts of $i$ respectively. If $\epsilon > 0$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Positive I Arbitrarily Small}, there exists $\ell \geq 0$ large enough such that $$\lVert ((s_g^*)^\ell \otimes 1_n) i_- (s_g^\ell \otimes 1_n) \rVert < \epsilon.$$ So by \eqref{equation: Paths In W Cutdown},
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\mu \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) & = & ((s_g^*)^\ell \otimes 1_n) \big( \mu \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) \big) (s_g^\ell \otimes 1_n)
\\
& \leq & ((s_g^*)^\ell \otimes 1_n) \big( \mu \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) + y^* y + i_+ \big) (s_g^\ell \otimes 1_n)
\\
& = & ((s_g^*)^\ell \otimes 1_n) \Big( \Big(c_{x_{ij}}(s_g) - \frac{1}{m} \delta_{i, j} \; p_v \Big)_{i, j = 1}^n + i_- \Big) (s_g^\ell \otimes 1_n)
\\
& \leq & \Big(c_{x_{ij}}(s_g) - \frac{1}{m} \delta_{i, j} \; p_v \Big)_{i, j = 1}^n + \epsilon \cdot (1_{C^*(E)} \otimes 1_n)
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
where $\delta_{i, j}$ is the Kronecker delta. Since this holds for arbitrary $\epsilon > 0$ and the subset of positive elements of a C*-algebra is always norm-closed, we find that
\begin{equation*}
\mu \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) \leq \Big(c_{x_{ij}}(s_g) -  \frac{1}{m} \delta_{i, j} \; p_v \Big)_{i, j = 1}^n
\end{equation*}
as positive elements in $M_n(C^*(E))$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Sg Cutdown}, there exists $k > 0$ large enough such that
\begin{equation*}
\big(c_{x_{ij}}(s_g) \big)_{i, j = 1}^n = ((s_g^*)^k \otimes 1_n) x (s_g^k \otimes 1_n). 
\end{equation*}
So
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\mu \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) & \leq & ((s_g^*)^k \otimes 1_n) \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \cdot (p_v \otimes 1_n) \Big) (s_g^k \otimes 1_n)
\\
& = & ((s_g^*)^k \otimes 1_n) \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \cdot ((1_{C^*(H)} + p_v) \otimes 1_n) \Big) (s_g^k \otimes 1_n)
\\
& = & ((s_g^*)^k \otimes 1_n) \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \cdot (1_{C^*(E)} \otimes 1_n) \Big) (s_g^k \otimes 1_n)
\\
& \leq & ((s_g^*)^k \otimes 1_n) \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ (s_g^k \otimes 1_n). 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Taking Cuntz classes, we obtain $n \cdot [p_v] \leq [(x - \frac{1}{m})_+]$. The reverse inequality follows by applying Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS} to the inequality
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)\Big(\Big[ \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \Big) = \Big[\pi \Big( \Big( x - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big) \Big] \leq n \cdot [\pi(p_v)] = \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(n \cdot [p_v])
\end{equation*}
and then using $n \cdot [p_v] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = n \cdot [p_v]$ from the Cuntz-Krieger relations.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
If $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ then by definition of the stack and Corollary \ref{corollary: Purely Large Order Stabilised}, $C^*(E)$ is a purely large extension of $C(\mathbb{T})$ by $I_H \cong C^*(H) \otimes K$. Conversely, assume that $C^*(E)$ is a purely large extension of $C(\mathbb{T})$ by $I_H$. We will first prove by induction that if $n > 0$ and $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+$  does not lie in $I_H \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ then $[x] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [x]$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
For the base case, assume that $n = 1$ so that $x \in C^*(E)_+ \backslash I_H$. Let $\epsilon > 0$ be small enough so that $(x - \epsilon)_+ \in C^*(E)_+ \backslash I_H$. Since $\mathcal{L}(E)$ is a dense *-subalgebra of $C^*(E)$, $\mathcal{L}(E)_+$ is dense in $C^*(E)_+$ and so by Lemma \ref{lemma: Countably Based}, there exist $y \in \mathcal{L}(E)_+$ and $m > 0$  such that 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Sup Dense}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] \leq \Big[\Big(y - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \leq [x].
\end{equation}
Since $[(x - \epsilon)_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ by assumption then $[(y - \frac{1}{m})_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Purely Large Axiom (O5)} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Span Matrix Cutdown Quotients To Projection}, 
\begin{equation*}
\Big[\Big(y - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = \Big[\Big(y - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big]. 
\end{equation*}
Hence by the LHS inequality of \eqref{equation: Sup Dense},
\begin{equation*}
[(x - \epsilon)_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}]  \leq \Big[\Big(y - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \leq [x].
\end{equation*}
Taking the supremum over $\epsilon > 0$, we obtain $[x] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [x]$. This proves the base case. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
For the inductive hypothesis, suppose that there exists $k > 0$ such that if $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_k(\mathbb{C}))_+$ does not lie in $I_H \otimes M_k(\mathbb{C})$ then $[x] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [x]$. Now recall the definition of $\Sigma_A$ from \eqref{equation: Scale}. We claim that if $[y] \in \Sigma_{M_k(C^*(E))} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ then $[y] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [y]$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
To this end, assume that $[y] \in \Sigma_{M_k(C^*(E))} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. Pick $\epsilon > 0$ small enough so that $[(y - \epsilon)_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Sandwich} applied to $M_k(C^*(E))$, there exists $b \in M_k(C^*(E))_+$ such that $[(y - \epsilon)_+] \ll [b] \ll [y]$. Since $[(y - \epsilon)_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ by construction then $[b] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ and by the inductive hypothesis, 
\begin{equation*}
[(y - \epsilon)_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] \leq [b] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [b] \leq [y]. 
\end{equation*}
Taking the supremum over all $\epsilon > 0$, $[y] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [y]$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now assume that $a \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_{k+1}(\mathbb{C}))_+$ does not lie in $I_H \otimes M_{k+1}(\mathbb{C})$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Countably Based}, there exist $z \in (z_{ij})_{i, j = 1}^{k+1} \in M_{k+1}(C^*(E))_+$ and $m > 0$ such that $z_{ij} \in \mathcal{L}(E)$ for $i, j \in \{1, 2, \dots, k+1 \}$ and 
\begin{equation*}
[(a - \epsilon)_+] \leq \Big[ \Big( z - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \leq [a]. 
\end{equation*}
Since $[(a - \epsilon)_+] \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ then $[(z - \frac{1}{m})_+] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. To see that $[(z - \frac{1}{m})_+]$ absorbs $\infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}]$, we split into three cases. First suppose that there does not exist a projection $p \in C(\mathbb{T}) \otimes K$ such that $[\pi((z - \frac{1}{m})_+)] = [p]$. Since $C^*(E)$ is a purely large extension of $C(\mathbb{T})$ by $I_H$ then by Proposition \ref{proposition: Purely Large Axiom (O5)},  $[(z - \frac{1}{m})_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [(z - \frac{1}{m})_+]$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Otherwise, if $[\pi((z - \frac{1}{m})_+)] = (k+1) \cdot [\pi(p_v)]$ then absorption  of $\infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}]$ follows from Lemma \ref{lemma: Span Matrix Cutdown Quotients To Projection}. Finally, if there exists $\ell \in \{1, 2, \dots, k \}$ such that $[\pi((z - \frac{1}{m})_+)] = \ell \cdot [\pi(p_v)]$ then by Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS} and the Cuntz-Krieger relations,
\begin{equation*}
\Big[ \Big( z - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \leq \ell \cdot [p_v] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = \ell \cdot [p_v] \leq k \cdot [p_v].
\end{equation*}
So $[(z - \frac{1}{m})_+] \in \Sigma_{M_k(C^*(E))} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ and by the previous claim, it absorbs $\infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}]$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Combining all three cases, we have $[(z - \frac{1}{m})_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [(z - \frac{1}{m})_+]$ and
\begin{equation*}
[(a - \epsilon)_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] \leq \Big[ \Big( z - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = \Big[ \Big( z - \frac{1}{m} \Big)_+ \Big] \leq [a].
\end{equation*}
By taking the supremum over $\epsilon > 0$, $[a] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] \leq [a]$. This completes the induction. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Finally assume that $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes K)_+ \backslash (I_H \otimes K)$. Once again, let $\epsilon > 0$ be small enough so that $[(x - \epsilon)_+] \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. There exists $n > 0$ such that $(x - \epsilon)_+ \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+$. By the previous result, $$[ (x - \epsilon)_+] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [(x - \epsilon)_+] \leq [x].$$ Taking the supremum over all $\epsilon > 0$, we have $[x] + \infty \cdot [1_{C^*(H)}] = [x]$. Proposition \ref{proposition: Stack Characterisation} finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lemma: QDS Purely Large}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. The extension in \eqref{equation: QDS Extension} is purely large.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Since the extension in \eqref{equation: QDS Extension} is essential, its associated Busby invariant $\beta: C(\mathbb{T}) \rightarrow \mathcal{Q}(C^*(E) \otimes K)$ is an injective *-homomorphism. We may view the multiplier algebra $\mathcal{M}(K)$ as a subalgebra of $\mathcal{M}(C^*(E) \otimes K)$ via the following chain of inclusions:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{M}(K) \cong \{ 1_{C^*(E)} \} \otimes \mathcal{M}(K) \subseteq C^*(E) \otimes \mathcal{M}(K) \subseteq \mathcal{M}(C^*(E) \otimes K). 
\end{equation*}
In particular, the Calkin algebra $\mathcal{Q}(K)$ is a unital subalgebra of $\mathcal{Q}(C^*(E) \otimes K)$ because by \eqref{equation: QDS Matrix Unit} and \eqref{equation: QDS Ideal Iso},
\begin{equation*}
1_{\mathcal{M}(C^*(E) \otimes K)} = {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} a_{ii} \in \mathcal{M}(K). 
\end{equation*}  
Now by \cite[Proposition 6.2]{HS02}, $\beta(\pi(s_g)) = \mu(1_{C^*(E)} \otimes s_g) \in \mathcal{Q}(K)$. Since $\pi(s_g)$ generates the quotient $C(\mathbb{T})$ then $\beta$ factors through $\mathcal{Q}(K)$. Consequently, if $x \in C(\mathbb{T})$ is non-zero then the ideal generated by $\beta(x) \neq 0$ in $\mathcal{Q}(K)$ contains the unit of $\mathcal{Q}(C^*(E) \otimes K)$. Therefore, $\beta$ is a full *-homomorphism and the extension in \eqref{equation: QDS Extension} is full. Moreover, the ideal $I_E \cong C^*(E) \otimes K$ is stable, $\sigma$-unital and satisfies the corona factorisation property by Proposition \ref{proposition: Graph CFP}. So by Theorem \ref{theorem: Kucerovsky Ng}, $C^*(S^2 E)$ is a purely large extension of $C(\mathbb{T})$ by $C^*(E) \otimes K$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Let $E$ and $H$ be as in Theorem \ref{introtheorem: General Cuntz Krieger} and suppose $v$ supports a single loop. By Proposition \ref{proposition: QDS Forcing}, there exists a finite graph $F$ such that $C^*(E)$ is stably isomorphic to $C^*(S^2 F)$ and $C^*(H)$ is stably isomorphic to $C^*(F)$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemma: QDS Purely Large} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Purely Large Circle Quotient},
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) & \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(S^2 F))
\\
& \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})
\\
& \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}). 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Same Open Subset Upstairs}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and suppose that there exists $v \in E^0$ such that $v$ supports a single loop $g$ and if $w \in E^0$ then $w \geq v$. Let $H = \{ w \in E^0 \; \vert \; v \not \geq w \} = E^0 \backslash \{ v \}$ and $U \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ be non-empty and open. As in Definition \ref{definition: Strictly Positive}, let $h_{v, U}$ be a strictly positive element of the ideal $$\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U} = I_{L(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}$$ and $\chi_U \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ denote the characteristic function of $U$. Then the isomorphism $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ from Theorem \ref{introtheorem: General Cuntz Krieger} sends $[h_{v, U}]$ to $\chi_U$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $\phi$ denote the Cu-isomorphism between $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ and $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ constructed in Proposition \ref{proposition: Stack Characterisation}, $\pi$ be the quotient map from $C^*(E)$ to $C(\mathbb{T})$ and $\rho$ be the map from $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ to $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ which is zero on $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$ and restricts to the identity on $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Stack Characterisation}, the following diagram commutes:
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Stack Commutative Diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \arrow[rr, "\phi"] \arrow[ddrr, swap, "\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)"] & & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \arrow[dd, "\rho"] \\
& & \\
& & \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation} 
Let $U$ be a non-empty, open subset of $\mathbb{T}$. If $U = \mathbb{T}$ then $h_{v, \mathbb{T}}$ is a strictly positive element of the gauge-invariant ideal $I_{L(v)} = C^*(E)$. By the Cuntz-Krieger relations on $E$, $$[h_{v, \mathbb{T}}] = {\sum}_{x \in E^0} [p_x] = [p_v]$$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. By commutativity of diagram \eqref{equation: Stack Commutative Diagram}, 
\begin{equation*}
(\rho \circ \phi)([h_{v, \mathbb{T}}]) = \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([p_v]) = [\pi(p_v)] = \chi_{\mathbb{T}} = \rho(\chi_{\mathbb{T}}). 
\end{equation*}
Now observe that as Cu-semigroups, 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Stack Quotient}
\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \cong \big(\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \big) / \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H)). 
\end{equation}
Hence by definition of a quotient Cu-semigroup (see Definition \ref{definition: Quotient Cu Semigroup}), $$\phi([h_{v, \mathbb{T}}]) \leq \chi_{\mathbb{T}} + \infty \cdot {\sum}_{x \in H} [p_x] = \chi_{\mathbb{T}}$$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ because $\chi_{\mathbb{T}} \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$. The reverse inequality follows from an analogous argument, where we note that $[h_{v, \mathbb{T}}] = [p_v] \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next assume that $U$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{T}$. Recall from Definition \ref{definition: Primitive Non Gauge Invariant} that if $t \in \mathbb{T}$ then $\mathcal{R}_{v, t}$ is the primitive, non-gauge-invariant ideal $\langle I_H, s_g - t p_v \rangle$. So if $t \in \mathbb{T} \backslash U$ then $\pi(\mathcal{R}_{v, t}) = \langle \pi(s_g) - t \pi(p_v) \rangle$ and 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Explicit Continuous Function}
(\pi(s_g) - t \pi(p_v) )^* (\pi(s_g) - t \pi(p_v) ) = 2 \pi(p_v) - t \pi(s_g)^* - t^* \pi(s_g). 
\end{equation}
The element on the RHS of \eqref{equation: Explicit Continuous Function} is the continuous function $z \mapsto 2 - t z^* - t^* z$, which is zero if and only if $z = t$. So
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{rank} \big(z \mapsto 2 - t z^* - t^* z \big) = 
\begin{cases}
0, \text{ if $z = t$,} \\
1, \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Now since the isomorphism $\operatorname{Cu}(C(\mathbb{T})) \cong \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ is implemented by the pointwise rank map, $[2 \pi(p_v) - t \pi(s_g)^* - t^* \pi(s_g)] = \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash \{ t \}}$ in $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Moreover, $2 \pi(p_v) - t \pi(s_g)^* - t^* \pi(s_g)$ is a full, positive element of the ideal $\langle \pi(s_g) - t \pi(p_v) \rangle$ and thus, as ideals of $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$, 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Primitive Ideal Cuntz Semigroup}
\operatorname{Cu}(\langle \pi(s_g) - t \pi(p_v) \rangle) = \big\{ f \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \; \vert \; f \leq \infty \cdot \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash \{ t \}} \big\}.
\end{equation}
Since \eqref{equation: Primitive Ideal Cuntz Semigroup} holds for $t \in \mathbb{T} \backslash U$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}(\pi(\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})) = \big\{ f \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \; \vert \; f \leq \infty \cdot \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} \big\}. 
\end{equation*}
Now since $h_{v, U}$ is a strictly positive element of the ideal $\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}$, $\pi(h_{v, U})$ is a strictly positive element of $\pi(\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})$ and 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}(\pi(\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})) = \big\{ f \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \; \vert \; f \leq \infty \cdot [\pi(h_{v, U})] \big\}.
\end{equation*}
So $\infty \cdot \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} = \infty \cdot [\pi(h_{v, U})]$. By taking infima and noting that $[\pi(h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})]$ and $\chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U}$ are both below $[\pi(p_v)]$ in $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$, we have
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
[\pi(h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})] & = & [\pi(h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})] \wedge [\pi(p_v)]
\\
& = & (\infty \cdot [\pi(h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})]) \wedge [\pi(p_v)]
\\
& = & (\infty \cdot \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} ) \wedge [\pi(p_v)]
\\
& = & \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} \wedge [\pi(p_v)] = \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U}. 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
So by commutativity of diagram \eqref{equation: Stack Commutative Diagram} once more, 
\begin{equation*}
(\rho \circ \phi)([h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}]) = \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}]) = [\pi(h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})] = \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} = \rho(\chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U}).
\end{equation*}
Once again by \eqref{equation: Stack Quotient}, the definition of the stack and the fact that $\chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U} \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$, $\phi([h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}]) \leq \chi_{\mathbb{T} \backslash U}$. The reverse inequality follows from \eqref{equation: Stack Quotient}, together with the fact that $\phi([h_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}]) \not \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$ (as otherwise, $s_g - t p_v \in \mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U} \subseteq I_H$ for $t \in \mathbb{T} \backslash U$).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{definition: Delta E}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Recalling the definition of the strictly positive element $h_{v, U}$ from Definition \ref{definition: Strictly Positive}, we define $\Delta_E(f)$ to be the following element of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Delta_E(f) & = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t, \; c(\check{v}) \neq 1} \Big( f(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big) \\
& + {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t, \; c(\check{v}) = 1} \Big( {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
Here, ${\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} [h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} ]$ is the supremum of the increasing sequence $$\Big\{ {\sum}_{i = 1}^{n} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] \Big\}_n.$$
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp}, any function $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ can be written as the supremum of an increasing sequence $\{ f_n \}_n$ where each $f_n$ is a finite sum of functions in Definition \ref{definition: Singletons}. The essential idea behind Definition \ref{definition: Delta E} is that the functions in Definition \ref{definition: Singletons} are mapped to linear combinations of Cuntz classes of strictly positive elements of ideals of $C^*(E)$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
To illustrate this, assume that $\check{v} \in S(E)^0$ satisfies $c(\check{v}) = 0$. Let $\mathcal{I}$ be the ideal lattice map defined in \eqref{equation: Ideal Lattice 2}, which is bijective by Theorem \ref{theorem: Ideal Lattice Iso}. To see where $\Delta_E$ sends the function $\theta_{\check{v}, 1}$, we first consider the ideal $\operatorname{Idl}(\theta_{\check{v}, 1})$ generated by $\theta_{\check{v}, 1}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ (see \eqref{equation: Singly Gen Ideal}). Use $\mathcal{I}$ to obtain the corresponding gauge-invariant ideal
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}^{-1}\big( \operatorname{Idl}(\theta_{\check{v}, 1}) \big) = I_{\{ v \}}
\end{equation*}
of $C^*(E)$. The map $\Delta_E$ then maps $\theta_{\check{v}, 1}$ to the Cuntz class of a strictly positive element of $I_{\{ v \}}$, which is $[p_v]$.  The cases where $c(\check{v}) \neq 0$ follow a similar principle. Moreover by Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp}, $f = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}$ and $\Delta_E$ is defined in such a way that
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Delta E Singleton}
\Delta_E(f) = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t}  \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{remark: Delta E Ideal}
Suppose that $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ and $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ is a proper hereditary subset of $S(E)^0$. By \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) = \langle \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^{\dagger} \rangle$ as hereditary subsets of $S(E)^0$, $$f \in \big\{ g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \; \big\vert \; \operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \langle \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^{\dagger} \rangle \big\}$$ and by Definition \ref{definition: Delta E}, $\Delta_E(f) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^{\dagger}})$. So by the contrapositive, if there does not exist a proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $\Delta_E(f) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ then $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ is not a proper hereditary subset of $S(E)^0$ and subsequently, $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) = S(E)^0$. This observation will play a major role in the proof of Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Delta E Cu Morphism}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. The map $\Delta_E: \operatorname{Cu}_E \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is a Cu-morphism.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
We first prove that $\Delta_E$ is additive. Suppose that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ and let $\check{v}$ be a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f + g) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. Similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: Cu E Minus H}, observe that if $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ then it must necessarily be a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. A similar statement holds for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. Without loss of generality, suppose that $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. If $\check{v} \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ then there is nothing to show. Otherwise, $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ and there are two cases to consider. Firstly, if $c(\check{v}) \neq 1$ then
{\small \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
& \Big( f(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big) + \Big( g(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big) \\
= & \Big( (f + g)(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
Secondly, if $c(\check{v}) = 1$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Same Open Subset Upstairs} applied to the graph $L(v)$,  
\begin{equation*}
{\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] + {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ g(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] = {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ (f + g)(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big]
\end{equation*}
in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(L(v)))$. Since $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(L(v))) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(v)})$ and $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(v)})$ is an ideal of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ then
\begin{equation*}
{\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] + {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ g(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] = {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ (f + g)(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big]
\end{equation*}
in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. Consequently, by summing over all terminal vertices of $\operatorname{supp}_0(f + g)$, we have $\Delta_E(f + g) = \Delta_E(f) + \Delta_E(g)$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next, we prove that $\Delta_E$ is order-preserving. Once again, assume that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ and $f \leq g$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. If $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ is not a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, there exists $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ such that $\check{v}$ admits a finite path to $\check{x}$. So for $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$, define
\begin{equation*}
O_{\check{x}} = \{ \check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t \; \vert \; \text{$\check{v} \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ and $\check{v} \geq \check{x}$} \}. 
\end{equation*}
We now divide the argument into two cases. First, suppose that every vertex in $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ is not a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ so that
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Orbit Union}
{\bigcup}_{\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} O_{\check{x}} = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t. 
\end{equation}
If $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ then by \eqref{equation: Subgraph Cuntz Semigroup}, $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(x)}) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H_x})  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(L(x) \backslash H_x))$. Observe that if $\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}$ then $\Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H_x})$. Hence by definition of the stack, 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Not Terminal Absorption}
{\sum}_{\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}) + \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{x}, g(\check{x})}) = \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{x}, g(\check{x})})
\end{equation}
in $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(x)})$ and thus, in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ as well. Since any Cuntz class in $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{H_x})$ is way-below any Cuntz class in $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(x)}) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H_x})$, we also have 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Not Terminal Inequality}
{\sum}_{\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}) \ll \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{x}, g(\check{x})})
\end{equation}
in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. Summing over all $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ in \eqref{equation: Not Terminal Inequality}, we obtain $\Delta_E(f) \leq \Delta_E(g)$ in this case by \eqref{equation: Delta E Singleton} and \eqref{equation: Orbit Union}. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Second, assume that there exists a vertex $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ which is also a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. If $c(\check{v}) \neq 1$ then by the assumption that $f \leq g$,
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Delta E Order No Loop}
f(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] \leq g(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w].
\end{equation} 
Note that if $c(\check{v}) = \infty$ then \eqref{equation: Delta E Order No Loop} follows from the fact that $f(\check{v}) = g(\check{v}) = \infty$. In the case where $c(\check{v}) = 0$, \eqref{equation: Delta E Order No Loop} follows from Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}. So by definition of $\Delta_E$, $\Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}) \leq \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, g(\check{v})})$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next, if $c(\check{v}) = 1$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} again, 
\begin{equation*}
{\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \chi_{\{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} = f(\check{v}) \leq g(\check{v}) = {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \chi_{\{ g(\check{v}) \geq i \}}
\end{equation*}
in $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Subsequently by Lemma \ref{lemma: Same Open Subset Upstairs},
\begin{equation*}
{\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] \leq {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ g(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big]
\end{equation*}  
in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ and $\Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})}) \leq \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, g(\check{v})})$ once more. Hence, by \eqref{equation: Delta E Singleton} and \eqref{equation: Not Terminal Absorption},
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
& & \Delta_E(f) = {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t}  \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{w}, f(\check{w})})
\\
& = & {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{w}, f(\check{w})}) + {\sum}_{\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} {\sum}_{\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})})
\\
& \leq & {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{w}, g(\check{w})}) + {\sum}_{\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} {\sum}_{\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})})
\\
& \leq & {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{w}, g(\check{w})}) + {\sum}_{\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} {\sum}_{\check{v} \in O_{\check{x}}} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, f(\check{v})})
\\
& = & {\sum}_{\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \Delta_E(\theta_{\check{w}, g(\check{w})}) = \Delta_E(g). 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Therefore, $\Delta_E$ is order-preserving. The proof that $\Delta_E$ preserves way-below is done similarly. Establishing this in the first case is done by summing over all $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t$ in \eqref{equation: Not Terminal Inequality} and using \ref{axiom: O3}. In the second case, the argument is nearly identical to the argument for order preservation, using Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below} in lieu of Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}. The key difference between the two arguments is that the way-below version of \eqref{equation: Delta E Order No Loop} is not immediate if $c(\check{v}) = \infty$. However, since $v$ supports multiple loops then by the Cuntz-Krieger relations, $\infty \cdot [p_v] = [p_v]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ and 
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
f(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] & = & \infty \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w]
\\
& = & [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w] = [p_v]
\\
& \ll & [p_v] 
\\
& \leq & g(\check{v}) \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w]. 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Finally, to see that $\Delta_E$ preserves suprema of increasing sequences, assume that $\{ f_n \}_{n > 0}$ is an increasing sequence in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ with supremum $f$. Since $S(E)$ only has finitely many hereditary subsets, there exists $k > 0$ such that if $\ell \geq 0$ then $$\operatorname{supp}_0(f_k) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f_{k+\ell}) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f).$$ Now if $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ then $f(\check{v}) = \sup_{n \geq k} f_n(\check{v})$. In particular, in the case where $c(\check{v}) = 1$, this claim follows from the fact that by Lemma \ref{lemma: Same Open Subset Upstairs},
\begin{equation*}
{\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big] = {\sup}_{n \geq k} {\sum}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \big[h_{v, \; \{ f_n(\check{v}) \geq i \}} \big]
\end{equation*}
in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. Since $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ satisfies \ref{axiom: O4} and $\Delta_E$ is order-preserving, $\Delta_E(f) = \sup_{n \geq k} \Delta_E(f_n) = \sup_{n > 0} \Delta_E(f_n)$. So $\Delta_E$ preserves suprema of increasing sequences and is therefore a Cu-morphism.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Ideal Square}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $H$ be a hereditary subset of $E^0$. The following diagram commutes:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
\operatorname{Cu}_H \arrow[r, "i_H"] \arrow[d, swap, "\Delta_H"] & \operatorname{Cu}_E \arrow[d, "\Delta_E"] \\
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H)) \arrow[r, swap, "\operatorname{Cu}(\iota)"] & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
where $i_H$ is the Cu-morphism in \eqref{equation: Inclusion} and $\iota$ is the inclusion map $I_H \hookrightarrow C^*(E)$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Assume that $\check{v} \in \langle H \rangle$ and $U \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ be non-empty and open. From the definitions, it follows from direct computation that if $c(\check{v}) = 0$ then $$(\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, 1}) = (\Delta_E \circ i_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, 1}) = [p_v],$$ if $c(\check{v}) = \infty$ then $$(\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \infty}) = (\Delta_E \circ i_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \infty}) = \infty \cdot [p_v] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w]$$ and if $c(\check{v}) = 1$ then $$(\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U}) = (\Delta_E \circ i_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U}) = [h_{v, U}] + {\sum}_{w \in L(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [p_w].$$ By Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp} and Proposition \ref{proposition: Delta E Cu Morphism}, the square commutes.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Quotient Square}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $H$ be a hereditary subset of $E^0$. The following diagram commutes:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
\operatorname{Cu}_E \arrow[r, "\rho_H"] \arrow[d, swap, "\Delta_E"] & \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H} \arrow[d, "\Delta_{E \backslash H}"] \\
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \arrow[r, swap, "\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)"] & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash H))
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
where $\rho_H$ is the Cu-morphism constructed in Lemma \ref{lemma: Cu E Minus H} and $\pi: C^*(E) \rightarrow C^*(E \backslash H)$ is the quotient map.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Assume that $\check{v} \in \langle E \rangle$ and $U \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ is non-empty and open. We may assume without loss of generality that $\check{v} \not \in \langle H \rangle$, as otherwise, there is nothing to show. Once again from the definitions, it follows by direct computation that if $c(\check{v}) = 0$ then $$(\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(\theta_{\check{v}, 1}) = (\Delta_{E \backslash H} \circ \rho_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, 1}) = [\pi(p_v)]$$ and if $c(\check{v}) = \infty$ then
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
& & (\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(\theta_{\check{v}, \infty}) = (\Delta_{E \backslash H} \circ \rho_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \infty}) 
\\
& = & \infty \cdot [\pi(p_v)] + {\sum}_{w \in L_{E \backslash H}(v), \; v \not \geq w} \infty \cdot [\pi(p_w)]
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
where $L_{E \backslash H}(v) = \{ x \in (E \backslash H)^0 \; \vert \; x \geq v \}$. Now if $c(\check{v}) = 1$ and $g$ is the single loop based at $v$ then 
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_E(\theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U}) = [h_{v, U}] + {\sum}_{w \in L_E(v) \backslash \{ v \}} \infty \cdot [p_w]
\end{equation*}
where $L_E(v) = \{ x \in E^0 \; \vert \; x \geq v \}$ and $h_{v, U}$ is a strictly positive element of the ideal $$I_{L_E(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{E, v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}.$$ For clarity, we have modified the notation established in Definition \ref{definition: Primitive Non Gauge Invariant} slightly to include the graph, emphasising that the above ideal is an ideal of $C^*(E)$. Now by combining \cite[II.5.1.4 (ii)]{Bla06} with surjectivity of $\pi$, we have that
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\pi ( I_{L_E(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{E, v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U} )  & = & \pi(I_{L_E(v)}) \cap \pi(\mathcal{R}_{E, v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U})
\\
& = & I_{L_{E \backslash H}(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{E \backslash H, v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}.
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Consequently, $\pi(h_{v, U})$ is a strictly positive element of $I_{L_{E \backslash H}(v)} \cap \mathcal{R}_{E \backslash H, v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}$ and by definition of $\Delta_{E \backslash H}$,
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
(\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(\theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U})  & = & \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)\Big( [h_{v, U}] + {\sum}_{w \in L_E(v) \backslash \{ v \}} \infty \cdot [p_w] \Big)
\\
& = & [\pi(h_{v, U})] + {\sum}_{w \in L_{E \backslash H}(v) \backslash \{ v \}} \infty \cdot [\pi(p_w)]
\\
& = & (\Delta_{E \backslash H} \circ \rho_H)(\theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U}). 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Again by Lemma \ref{lemma: Singleton Decomp} and Proposition \ref{proposition: Delta E Cu Morphism}, the square commutes.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Base Case}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Suppose that $C^*(E)$ has gauge length one. Then the Cu-morphism $\Delta_E: \operatorname{Cu}_E \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Length}, the skeleton $S(E)$ has exactly one vertex, which we denote by $\check{v}$. There are now three cases to consider. If $c(\check{v}) = 0$ then $E$ consists of a single source vertex $v$. By definition of $\Delta_E$ (see Definition \ref{definition: Delta E}) and the fact that $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \cong \overline{\mathbb{N}}$, it is clear that $\Delta_E$ is a Cu-isomorphism in this case. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next, suppose that $c(\check{v}) = \infty$. By the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Simple}, $C^*(E)$ is simple purely infinite and the map $\Delta_E$ is explicitly given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{matrix}
\Delta_E: & \operatorname{Cu}_E & \rightarrow & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \\
& \big(\check{v} \mapsto \infty \big) & \mapsto & \infty \cdot [p_v]. 
\end{matrix}
\end{equation*}
Since the only non-zero element of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is the function $\check{v} \mapsto \infty$ and $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is isomorphic to $\{ 0, \infty \}$, $\Delta_E$ is a Cu-isomorphism in this case. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Finally, suppose that $c(\check{v}) = 1$. By standing assumption \ref{property: S3}, $E$ consists of a single vertex $v$ which supports a single loop and so $C^*(E) \cong C(\mathbb{T})$. If $U \subseteq \mathbb{T}$ is non-empty and open then $\Delta_E$ is explicitly the map
\begin{equation*}
\begin{matrix}
\Delta_E: & \operatorname{Cu}_E & \rightarrow & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \\
& \theta_{\check{v}, \chi_U} & \mapsto & [h_{v, U}]
\end{matrix}
\end{equation*}
where $h_{v, U}$ is a strictly positive element of the ideal $\mathcal{R}_{v, \mathbb{T} \backslash U}$ (see Definition \ref{definition: Strictly Positive}). The isomorphism $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \cong \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ sends $[h_{v, U}]$ to $\chi_U$. Consequently, $\Delta_E$ is a Cu-isomorphism, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
First observe that it suffices to prove Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso} in the special case where $E$ consists of a single connected component. Indeed, suppose that $E = E_1 \sqcup E_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup E_m$ where $m > 1$ and for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, m \}$, $E_j$ is a connected subgraph. It is straightforward to check that 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}_E \cong {\bigoplus}_{j = 1}^m \operatorname{Cu}_{E_j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \Delta_E = \Delta_{E_1} \oplus \dots \oplus \Delta_{E_m}. 
\end{equation*}
So if Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso} is true for graphs consisting of a single connected component then $\Delta_{E_j}$ is a Cu-isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_{E_j}$ to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E_j))$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, m \}$. Therefore, $\Delta_E$ is an isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ to $${\bigoplus}_{j = 1}^m \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E_j)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$$ which gives Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso} in general. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Without loss of generality, assume that $E$ consists of a single connected component. We will prove that $\Delta_E$ is a Cu-isomorphism. The base case where $C^*(E)$ has gauge length one is done by Lemma \ref{lemma: Base Case}. For the inductive hypothesis, assume that there exists $k > 0$ such that for a finite graph $F$ which satisfies the standing assumptions, has gauge length $k$  and consists of a single connected component, $\Delta_F$ is a Cu-isomorphism. Suppose that $C^*(E)$ has gauge length $k + 1$. Then there exists an ascending chain of gauge-invariant ideals
\begin{equation*}
\{ 0 \} = I_0 \subseteq I_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq I_k \subseteq I_{k+1} = C^*(E)
\end{equation*}
such that if $j \in \{0, 1, \dots, k \}$ and $H_j$ is the hereditary subset of $E^0$ corresponding to $I_j$ then $C^*(H_{j+1} \backslash H_j)$ is gauge-simple. In particular, $C^*(H_1)$ is gauge-simple. Let $\pi: C^*(E) \rightarrow C^*(E \backslash H_1)$ be the quotient map. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
$\Delta_E$ is an \textbf{order-embedding:} \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Let $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ be such that $\Delta_E(f) \leq \Delta_E(g)$. First, suppose that there exists a proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $\Delta_E(g) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. Then $\Delta_E(f) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$ and by definition of $\Delta_E$ (see Definition \ref{definition: Delta E}), $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ both lie in $\langle H \rangle$. Since $H$ is a proper hereditary subset of $E^0$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Length}, $C^*(H)$ has gauge length $\lvert S(H)^0 \rvert < \lvert S(E)^0 \rvert = k+1$. So if $H$ consists of a single connected component then by the inductive hypothesis, $\Delta_H$ is a Cu-isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_H$ to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H)) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. On the other hand, if $H$ consists of multiple disjoint connected subgraphs then the inductive hypothesis tells that on each connected subgraph $G$ of $H$, $\Delta_G$ is a Cu-isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_G$ to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(G))$. Then by taking direct sums, $\Delta_H$ is still a Cu-isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_H$ to $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Using \eqref{equation: Ideal In Terms Of Support}, we may view $f$ and $g$ as elements of $\operatorname{Cu}_H$. So $(\Delta_E \circ i_H)(f) \leq (\Delta_E \circ i_H)(g)$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma: Ideal Square}, $(\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(f) \leq (\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(g)$. In particular, $\Delta_H(f) \leq \Delta_H(g)$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ and hence, in $\operatorname{Cu}(I_H) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$ as well. Since $\Delta_H$ is a Cu-isomorphism then $f \leq g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_H$ and by applying the map $i_H$, $f \leq g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now assume that there is no proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $\Delta_E(g) \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. Then $(\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(f) \leq (\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(g)$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma: Quotient Square}, $(\Delta_{E \backslash H_1} \circ \rho_{H_1})(f) \leq (\Delta_{E \backslash H_1} \circ \rho_{H_1})(g)$. By the inductive hypothesis, $\Delta_{E \backslash H_1}$ is a Cu-isomorphism. So $\rho_{H_1}(f) \leq \rho_{H_1}(g)$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H_1}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Observe that by Remark \ref{remark: Delta E Ideal}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(g) = S(E)^0$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Length}, $S(H_1)$ consists of a single vertex $\check{w}$. If $\check{w}$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g) = S(E)^0$ and $v \in E^0$ satisfies $w \geq v$ then $v \geq w$ and $v \in H_1$. Coupled with the fact that $H_1$ is hereditary, we see that $H_1$ is an isolated subgraph of $E$. Since $E$ consists of exactly one connected component then by the contrapositive, $\check{w}$ cannot be a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$. So by Definition \ref{definition: Cu E}, $g(\check{w}) = \infty$. Together with the Cu-isomorphism $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H_1} \cong \operatorname{Cu}_E /\operatorname{Cu}_{H_1}$ from Proposition \ref{proposition: First Iso Thm Cu E} and the inequality $\rho_{H_1}(f) \leq \rho_{H_1}(g)$, there exists $h \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $\operatorname{supp}_0(h) \subseteq \langle H_1 \rangle = \{ \check{w} \}$ and $f \leq g + h = g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. Therefore, $\Delta_E$ is an order-embedding. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
$\Delta_E$ is \textbf{surjective:} \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Assume that $[x] \in \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. Firstly, if there exists a proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $[x] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H))$ then by the inductive hypothesis, $\Delta_H$ is a Cu-isomorphism and there exists $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_H$ such that $\Delta_H(f) = [x]$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Ideal Square}, $i_H(f) = f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ satisfies
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_E(f) = (\Delta_E \circ i_H)(f) = (\operatorname{Cu}(\iota) \circ \Delta_H)(f) = [\iota(x)] = [x]. 
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, suppose that there is no such proper hereditary subset $H$. If there exists a proper hereditary subset $H'$ of $(E \backslash H_1)^0$ such that $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([x]) = [\pi(x)] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H'})$ then $[\pi(x)] \leq \infty \cdot {\sum}_{v \in H'} [\pi(p_v)]$ and by Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS}, $$[x] \leq \infty \cdot \Big[{\sum}_{v \in H' \sqcup H_1} p_v \Big]$$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. Thus, $H' \sqcup H_1$ is a proper hereditary subset of $E^0$ such that $[x] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H' \sqcup H_1})$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
By the contrapositive, there is no proper hereditary subset $H'$ of $(E \backslash H_1)^0$ such that $[\pi(x)] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{H'})$. Since $\Delta_{E \backslash H_1}$ is a Cu-isomorphism by the inductive hypothesis, there exists $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H_1}$ such that $\Delta_{E \backslash H_1}(g) = [\pi(x)]$. So by Remark \ref{remark: Delta E Ideal} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Cu E Minus H}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(g) = S(E \backslash H_1)^0$ and $$g' = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g)_t} \theta_{\check{v}, g(\check{v})} + \infty \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}}$$ is an element of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $\operatorname{supp}_0(g') = S(E)^0$ and $\rho_{H_1}(g') = g$ (recall the definition of $\delta_{\check{w}}$ from \eqref{equation: Delta V}). By Lemma \ref{lemma: Quotient Square}, 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Need To Lift}
(\operatorname{Cu}(\pi) \circ \Delta_E)(g') = (\Delta_{E \backslash H_1} \circ \rho_{H_1})(g') = \Delta_{E \backslash H_1}(g) = \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([x]). 
\end{equation}
We claim that $\Delta_E(g') = [x]$. Since $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([x]) \leq \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(\Delta_E(g'))$ then by Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS}, 
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
[x] & \leq & \Delta_E(g') + \infty \cdot [p_w]
\\
& = & \Delta_E(g) + \Delta_E(\infty \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}}) + \infty \cdot [p_w]
\\
& = & \Delta_E(g) + \Delta_E(\infty \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}}) + \Delta_E(\infty \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}})
\\
& = & \Delta_E(g) + \Delta_E(\infty \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}})
\\
& = & \Delta_E(g'). 
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
To show that the reverse inequality holds, we will take advantage of the fact that $I_1$ is gauge-simple. There are two possible cases to consider. First, assume that $I_1$ is simple purely infinite. Then $C^*(H_1)$ is simple purely infinite and subsequently, $[p_w]$ is a properly infinite element of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: Purely Infinite Properly Infinite}. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
We will now show that $[x] + [p_w] = [x]$. For simplicity, first assume that $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+$. Since the lone vertex $\check{w}$ of $S(H_1)$ is not a terminal vertex for $S(E)^0$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, there exists $\check{v} \in S(E)^0$ such that $\check{v}$ is terminal and $\check{w} \geq \check{v}$. Let $1_n$ denote the unit of $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $p_S = \sum_{a \in S} p_a$ for arbitrary $S \subseteq E^0$. Then 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Not In Ideal Decomp}
\begin{split}
x & = (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) + (p_{E^0 \backslash R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n)   \\
& + (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n)  x (p_{E^0 \backslash R(v)} \otimes 1_n) + (p_{E^0 \backslash R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{E^0 \backslash R(v)} \otimes 1_n).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Since $R(v) = \{ a \in E^0 \; \vert \; v \geq a \}$ and $\check{v}$ is terminal for $S(E)^0$ then $R(v) \subseteq L(v)$ and subsequently, $$(p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) \in (I_{L(v)} \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+.$$  Since $w \geq v$ and $w \neq v$ then $v$ cannot be a source vertex. So by standing assumptions \ref{property: S1} and \ref{property: S2}, $v$ supports at least one cycle. By Theorem \ref{introtheorem: General Cuntz Krieger}, the set $G = \{ x \in L(v) \; \vert \; v \not \geq x \}$ is a hereditary subset of $L(v)$ and
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Cuntz Stack Computation}
\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(v)}) \cong \operatorname{Cu}(I_G)  \;
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.125, line width = 0.7pt]
                      
        \draw (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);
                                           
        \draw (0,1) rectangle (1,2);
    \end{tikzpicture}
\;  \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(L(v) \backslash G))
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(L(v) \backslash G))$ is either $\{0, \infty \}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Now since $G \subseteq E^0 \backslash R(v)$ then $$(p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) \not \in I_{G} \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$$ as otherwise by \eqref{equation: Not In Ideal Decomp}, $x \in I_{E^0 \backslash R(v)} \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$, which would contradict our assumption that there is no proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $[x] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. So $$[(p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n)] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(v)}) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(I_G).$$ Now let $e_{11} \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ be the matrix with a 1 in the top left corner and zeros elsewhere. By \eqref{equation: Cuntz Stack Computation} and the fact that $[p_w] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_G)$,
\begin{equation*}
[p_w] = [p_w \otimes e_{11}] \leq [(p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n) x (p_{R(v)} \otimes 1_n)]
\end{equation*}
in the ideal $\operatorname{Cu}(I_{L(v)})$ and hence, in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ as well. Since $[p_w]$ is properly infinite and $[p_w] \leq [x]$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Polar Part Absorbed} with $A = C^*(E) \otimes K$, $x \oplus (p_w \otimes e_{11}) \precsim x$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
So we have proved that if $n > 0$ and $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C}))_+$ then $[x] + [p_w] = [x]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$. This is extended to the case where $x \in (C^*(E) \otimes K)_+$ by repeating the above argument for $(x - \epsilon)_+$ where $\epsilon > 0$ is chosen small enough so that there is no proper hereditary subset $H$ of $E^0$ such that $[(x - \epsilon)_+] \in \operatorname{Cu}(I_H)$. Now to see that $\Delta_E(g') \leq [x]$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$, recall from \eqref{equation: Need To Lift} that $\operatorname{Cu}(\pi)(\Delta_E(g')) \leq \operatorname{Cu}(\pi)([x])$ in $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash H_1))$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS} and the fact that $[x]$ absorbs $[p_w]$, 
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_E(g') \leq [x] + \infty \cdot [p_w] = [x]. 
\end{equation*}
Therefore, we have $\Delta_E(g') = [x]$ in this case. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
For the second case, assume that $I_1$ has stable rank one. By the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: Axiom O2}, there exists a rapidly increasing sequence $\{ h_n \}_{n > 0}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that for $n > 0$, $\operatorname{supp}_0(h_n) = \operatorname{supp}_0(g') = S(E)^0$ and $\sup_{n > 0} h_n = g'$. Now if $k > 0$ then by Theorem \ref{theorem: CRS} and the fact that $\Delta_E$ is a Cu-morphism (see Proposition \ref{proposition: Delta E Cu Morphism}),
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_E(h_k) \ll \Delta_E(g') \leq [x] + \infty \cdot [p_w]. 
\end{equation*}
So there exists $\ell > 0$ such that $\Delta_E(h_k) \leq [x] + \ell \cdot [p_w]$. Now since $\check{w}$ is not a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(h_k) = S(E)^0$ then $h_k(\check{w}) = \infty$ and 
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_E(h_k) + \ell \cdot [p_w] = \Delta_E(h_k + \ell \cdot \theta_{\check{w}, \delta_{\check{w}}}) = \Delta_E(h_k) \leq  [x] + \ell \cdot [p_w]. 
\end{equation*}
By the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: Base Case}, $H_1$ is either a single vertex or a single vertex supporting exactly one loop. Therefore by \eqref{equation: Full Corner Iso}, the corner $$p_w C^*(E) p_w = p_w I_1 p_w \cong C^*(H_1)$$ has stable rank one and by Theorem \ref{theorem: SR1 Corner Positive Cancellation}, $\Delta_E(h_k) \leq [x]$. Since $\Delta_E$ preserves suprema of increasing sequences, $$\Delta_E(g') = {\sup}_{n > 0} \Delta_E(h_n) \leq [x].$$ Therefore, $\Delta_E(g') \leq [x]$ and $[x] = \Delta_E(g')$ in general. Hence, $\Delta_E$ is surjective, which completes the proof of Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
Let $M$ be a positively ordered monoid and $x, y \in M$. Define $x <_s y$ if and only if there exists $k > 0$ such that $(k+1) x \leq k y$. Now let $n \geq 0$. $M$ is said to have the \textbf{$n$-comparison property} if for $x, y_0, y_1, \dots, y_n \in M$ satisfying $x <_s y_j$ for $j \in \{0, 1, \dots, n \}$, we have $x \leq \sum_{j = 0}^n y_j$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Assume that $E$ is a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Let $f, g_0, g_1 \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ be such that $f <_s g_0$ and $f <_s g_1$. There exist $k_0, k_1 > 0$ such that $(k_0 + 1) \cdot f \leq k_0 \cdot g_0$ and $(k_1 + 1) \cdot f \leq k_1 \cdot g_1$. Hence if $j \in \{0, 1 \}$ then $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$. Now let $\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g_0) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(g_1)$ be terminal and satisfy $c(\check{w}) \neq \infty$. If $\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g_0) \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g_1)$ then $\check{w}$ is a terminal vertex for both $\operatorname{supp}_0(g_0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}_0(g_1)$. So by Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, 
\begin{equation*}
(k_0 + 1) \cdot f(\check{w}) \leq k_0 \cdot g_0(\check{w}) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (k_1 + 1) \cdot f(\check{w}) \leq k_1 \cdot g_1(\check{w}). 
\end{equation*}
Since $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ both have the 1-comparison property, $f(\check{w}) \leq g_0(\check{w}) + g_1(\check{w})$ in this case. Otherwise, if there exists $j \in \{0, 1 \}$ such that $\check{w} \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$ then $\check{w} \not \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and $f(\check{w}) = 0 \leq g_0(\check{w}) + g_1(\check{w})$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative} once more, $f \leq g_0 + g_1$ and so $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ has the 1-comparison property. The second statement follows from Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph}.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{remark: Graph CFP 2}
In \cite[Definition 2.11]{OPR12}, a property called $\omega$-comparison was defined for positively ordered monoids which contain suprema of all increasing sequences. Notably, the definition of the $\omega$-comparison property applies to Cu-semigroups, and the $n$-comparison property for some $n \geq 0$ implies the $\omega$-comparison property. If $E$ is an arbitrary finite graph, then by Corollary \ref{introcorollary: Cu E One Comparison}, $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ has the $\omega$-comparison property. By \cite[Proposition 2.17]{OPR12}, $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ has the corona factorisation property for semigroups and consequently, $C^*(E)$ has the corona factorisation property by \cite[Theorem 5.11]{OPR12}. This is consistent with Proposition \ref{proposition: Graph CFP}. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Furthermore, by using the characterisation of an inductive limit of Cu-semigroups from \cite[Lemma 3.8]{TV22}, it is straightforward, but tedious to check that the 1-comparison property is preserved by taking inductive limits of Cu-semigroups. By \cite[Lemma 3.3]{AMP07} and \cite[Theorem 2]{CEI08}, the Cuntz semigroup of any graph C*-algebra from a row-finite graph is an inductive limit of Cuntz semigroups of unital graph C*-algebras. Hence, such a graph C*-algebra must also have the corona factorisation property. This is extended to any graph C*-algebra by Drinen-Tomforde desingularisation (see \cite[Theorem 2.11]{DT05}). The fact that any graph C*-algebras has the corona factorisation property is known to experts; see the remark preceding \cite[Proposition 6.1]{ERR13}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{definition: Cu Covering Dimension}
Let $S$ be a Cu-semigroup and $n \geq 0$. We say that $\dim S \leq n$ if for $r > 0$ and $x', x, y_1, \dots, y_r \in S$ satisfying $$x' \ll x \ll y_1 + \dots + y_r,$$ there exist $z_{j, k} \in S$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n \}$ such that the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n \}$ then $z_{j, k} \ll y_j$.
\item $x' \ll \sum_{j = 1}^r \sum_{k = 0}^n z_{j, k}$.
\item If $k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n \}$ then $\sum_{j = 1}^r z_{j, k} \ll x$. 
\end{enumerate}
If there is no such $n \geq 0$ such that $\dim S \leq n$ then we set $\dim S = \infty$. The \textbf{covering dimension} of $S$, denoted by $\dim S$, is the smallest $n \geq 0$ such that $\dim S \leq n$.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Way Below 2}
Let $(S, c)$ be a skeleton and $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_S$. Then $f \ll g$ if and only if the following statements are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g)$.
