\item Suppose that $w\in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g)$ and $c(w) \neq \infty$. Then $f(w) \ll g(w)$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Cu E Covering Dimension}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then
\begin{equation*}
\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E = 
\begin{cases}
0, \text{ if $E$ satisfies Condition (K),} \\
1, \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
First suppose that $E$ satisfies Condition (K). By \cite[Theorem 4.6]{JPS01}, $C^*(E)$ has real rank zero and subsequently by \cite[Theorem 5.7]{TV22} and Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}, $\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E = 0$. Now suppose that $E$ does not satisfy Condition (K) so that there exist vertices in $E$ which support a single loop. To see that $\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E \leq 1$, assume that $r > 0$ and $f', f, g_1, \dots, g_r \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ satisfy $$f' \ll f \ll g_1 + \dots + g_r.$$ By the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: Axiom O2}, there exists a rapidly increasing sequence $\{ h_n \}_{n > 0}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that for $n > 0$, $\operatorname{supp}_0(h_n) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and $\sup_{n > 0} h_n = f$. Since $f' \ll f$, there exists $h \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $f' \leq h \ll f$ and $\operatorname{supp}_0(h) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
We claim that if $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ and $c(\check{v}) \neq \infty$ then there exist elements $z_{j, k, v}$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ in either $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ then $z_{j, k, v} \ll g_j(v)$, 
\item $h(v) \ll \sum_{j = 1}^r \sum_{k = 0}^1 z_{j, k, v}$, 
\item if $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ then $\sum_{j = 1}^r z_{j, k, v} \ll f(v)$. 
\end{enumerate}
To this end, assume that $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ is such that $c(\check{v}) \neq \infty$. If $\check{v}$ is also a terminal vertex for $\bigcup_{i = 1}^r \operatorname{supp}_0(g_i)$ then by Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below}, we have in either $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$
\begin{equation*}
h(\check{v}) \ll f(\check{v}) \ll g_1(\check{v}) + \dots + g_r(\check{v}). 
\end{equation*}
Now recall that $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ both have covering dimension at most one by \cite[Theorem 5.7]{TV22} and \cite[Corollary 4.8]{TV22} respectively. By Definition \ref{definition: Cu Covering Dimension}, there exist $z_{j, k, v}$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ which collectively satisfy the three conditions outlined above. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next assume that $\check{v}$ is not a terminal vertex for $\bigcup_{i = 1}^r \operatorname{supp}_0(g_i)$. Then $h(\check{v}) \ll f(\check{v})$ and $g_1(\check{v}) + \dots + g_r(\check{v}) = \infty$. If $f(\check{v}) \neq \infty$ then $$h(\check{v}) \ll f(\check{v}) \ll \infty = g_1(\check{v}) + \dots + g_r(\check{v})$$ in either $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Once again by Definition \ref{definition: Cu Covering Dimension}, there exist $z_{j, k, v}$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ with the three properties we are after. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
If $f(\check{v}) = \infty$ then let $\ell \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ be such that $g_\ell(\check{v}) = \infty$. We have $$h(\check{v}) \ll f(\check{v}) = \infty = g_\ell(\check{v})$$ and so there exists $z_{\ell, 0, v}$ such that $h(\check{v}) \ll z_{\ell, 0, v} \ll g_\ell(\check{v})$ in either $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Now if $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$, $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ and $(j, k) \neq (\ell, 0)$ then define $z_{j, k, v} = 0$. In this way, the family of elements $\{ z_{j, k, v} \}_{j, k}$ satisfies the three properties we are after. This proves the claim.\newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now if $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ then define $S_j = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$ and
\begin{equation*}
\zeta_{j, k} = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in S_j} \theta_{\check{v}, z_{j, k, v}}
\end{equation*}
with the convention that $\theta_{\check{v}, z_{j, k, v}} = 0$ if $z_{j, k, v} = 0$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, 
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k}) & \subseteq & {\bigcup}_{\check{v} \in S_j} L_{S(E)}(\check{v})
\\
& \subseteq & \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j) \cap {\bigcup}_{\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t} L_{S(E)}(\check{v})
\\
& = & \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j) \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(f).
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Furthermore, if $\check{v}, \check{w} \in S_j$ are distinct then $\check{w} \not \in L_{S(E)}(\check{v})$ because $\check{v}$ and $\check{w}$ are both terminal vertices for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. Since the vertex support of $\theta_{\check{v}, z_{j, k, v}}$ is $L_{S(E)}(\check{v})$ then 
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Zeta Evaluation}
\zeta_{j, k}(\check{w}) = {\sum}_{\check{v} \in S_j} \theta_{\check{v}, z_{j, k, v}}(w) = z_{j, k, w}. 
\end{equation}
Next, observe that
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0 \Big( {\sum}_{j, k} \zeta_{j, k} \Big) = {\bigcup}_{j, k} \operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k}) \subseteq  \operatorname{supp}_0(f). 
\end{equation*}
To see that the reverse inclusion holds, assume that $\check{v} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. By Lemma \ref{lemma: Hereditary Terminal}, there exists $\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ such that $\check{v} \geq \check{w}$. By construction of the elements $z_{j, k, w}$, we know that $h(\check{w}) \ll \sum_{j, k} z_{j, k, w}$ in either $\overline{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$. Now since $\operatorname{supp}_0(h) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ then $h(\check{w}) \neq 0$ and so, there exist $j' \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k' \in \{0, 1 \}$ such that $0 \neq z_{j', k', w} = \zeta_{j', k'}(\check{w})$. Since $\check{v} \in L_S(\check{w})$ then $\zeta_{j', k'}(\check{v}) = \infty$. This gives the reverse inclusion and so
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Zeta Support}
\operatorname{supp}_0 \Big( {\sum}_{j, k} \zeta_{j, k} \Big) = \operatorname{supp}_0(f) = \operatorname{supp}_0(h).
\end{equation}
We will now show that the first property in Definition \ref{definition: Cu Covering Dimension} is satisfied. Assume that $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$. We know that $\operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$. If $\check{w} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k})$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$ then by definition of $\zeta_{j, k}$, there exists $\check{x} \in S_j$ such that $\check{w} \geq \check{x}$. But since $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$ then $\check{w} = \check{x} \in S_j$ and $\zeta_{j, k}(\check{w}) = z_{j, k, w} \ll g_j(\check{w})$ by \eqref{equation: Zeta Evaluation}. So by Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below 2}, we have $\zeta_{j, k} \ll g_j$ for $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ and $k \in \{0, 1 \}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
To see that the second property in Definition \ref{definition: Cu Covering Dimension} is satisfied, observe that if $\check{a} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(h)_t = \operatorname{supp}_0(f)_t$ then
{\small \begin{equation*}
h(\check{a}) \ll {\sum}_{j, k} z_{j, k, a} = {\sum}_{j, k} \theta_{\check{a}, z_{j, k, a}}(\check{a}) \leq {\sum}_{j, k} {\sum}_{v \in S_j} \theta_{\check{v}, z_{j, k, v}}(\check{a}) = {\sum}_{j, k} \zeta_{j, k}(\check{a}). 
\end{equation*}}
By \eqref{equation: Zeta Support} and Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below 2}, $h \ll \sum_{j, k} \zeta_{j, k}$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. Since $f' \leq h$ then $f' \ll \sum_{j, k} \zeta_{j, k}$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Now we verify that the third property in Definition \ref{definition: Cu Covering Dimension} holds. First observe that if $k \in \{0, 1 \}$ then
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0 \Big( {\sum}_{j = 1}^r \zeta_{j, k} \Big) \subseteq {\bigcup}_{j = 1}^r \operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f).
\end{equation*}
Assume that $\check{x} \in \operatorname{supp}_0 \Big( {\sum}_{j = 1}^r \zeta_{j, k} \Big)$ is a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. If $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, r \}$ then by \eqref{equation: Zeta Evaluation} and the inclusion $\operatorname{supp}_0(\zeta_{j, k}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(g_j)$, 
\begin{equation*}
\zeta_{j, k}(\check{x}) = 
\begin{cases}
z_{j, k, x}, \text{ if $\check{x} \in S_j$,} \\
0, \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Therefore, $${\sum}_{j = 1}^r \zeta_{j, k}(\check{x}) \leq {\sum}_{j = 1}^r z_{j, k, x} \ll f(\check{x})$$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma: Way Below 2}, $\sum_{j = 1}^r \zeta_{j, k} \ll f$ for $k \in \{0, 1 \}$. So $\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E \leq 1$. Finally, by considering functions of the form $\theta_{\check{v}, f}$ where $c(\check{v}) = 1$ and $f \in \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ is non-zero, $\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E \neq 0$ because $\dim \operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}}) \neq 0$. So $\dim \operatorname{Cu}_E = 1$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By \cite[Theorem 2.11]{DT05}, it suffices to prove Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Covering Dimension} in the case where $E$ is row-finite. So assume that $E$ is a row-finite graph. Then $C^*(E)$ can be written as an inductive limit of unital graph C*-algebras $\{ C^*(E_i) \}_{i > 0}$ such that if $i > 0$ then $E_i$ is a subgraph of $E$; see for instance, \cite[Lemma 3.1]{AMP07} and \cite[Lemma 3.3]{AMP07}. If $E$ satisfies Condition (K) then $E_i$ must also satisfy Condition (K) for $i > 0$. So by Proposition \ref{proposition: Cu E Covering Dimension} and \cite[Proposition 3.10]{TV22},
\begin{equation*}
\dim \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) \leq {\liminf}_{i > 0} \dim \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E_i)) = 0. 
\end{equation*}
If $E$ does not satisfy Condition (K) then by a similar argument, the covering dimension of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ is at most 1.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{definition: RPL}
Let 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow[r] & I \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r] & B \arrow[r] & 0 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
be an extension of C*-algebras and $J$ be an ideal of $I$. The extension is said to be \textbf{purely large relative to} $J$ if for $a \in J_+$ and $b \in A_+ \backslash I$, $a \precsim b$.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lemma: RPL Extensions}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Let $H$ be a hereditary subset of $E^0$ such that the quotient $C^*(E \backslash H)$ is gauge-simple. Let $H'$ be the hereditary set
\begin{equation*}
H' = \{ w \in H \; \vert \; \text{There exists $x \in E^0 \backslash H$ such that $w \geq x$} \}. 
\end{equation*}
If $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \backslash \mathcal{I}(I_H)$ and $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ is such that $\operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \langle H' \rangle$ then $f + g = f$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
By \eqref{equation: Ideal In Terms Of Support}, $\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \not \subseteq \langle H \rangle$ and $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \not \subseteq H$ as hereditary subsets of $E^0$, where $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ is defined in \eqref{equation: Dagger}. We claim that $H' \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$. To this end, assume that $w \in H'$. Then $w \in H$ and there exists $x \in E^0 \backslash H$ such that $w \geq x$. Since $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger \not \subseteq H$ then there exists $z \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ such that $z \in E^0 \backslash H$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
By assumption, the quotient $C^*(E \backslash H)$ is gauge-simple. So by Lemma \ref{lemma: Gauge Simple} and the fact that the subgraph $E \backslash H$ satisfies the standing assumptions, $\check{x} = \check{z}$. So $w \geq x \geq z$ in $E$ and since $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$ is a hereditary subset of $E^0$, $w \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$. So $H' \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^\dagger$. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
Next, we claim that if $\check{a} \in \langle H' \rangle_t$ then $f(\check{a}) = \infty$. Since $H' \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f)^{\dagger}$ then by \eqref{equation: Hereditary Skeleton}, $\langle H' \rangle \subseteq \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and $\check{a} \in \operatorname{supp}_0(f)$. To see that $\check{a}$ is not a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$, observe that in $E$, $a$ lies in $H'$ and thus, admits a finite path to $z$. But since $z \not \in H$, $z$ cannot admit a finite path back to $a$. Hence, $\check{a} \geq \check{z}$ and $\check{z} \not \geq \check{a}$ in $S(E)$. So $\check{a}$ is not a terminal vertex for $\operatorname{supp}_0(f)$ and $f(\check{a}) = \infty$. Consequently, $f$ is infinite-valued on all of $\langle H' \rangle$ and hence, $f$ absorbs any function $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $\operatorname{supp}_0(g) \subseteq \langle H' \rangle$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Extension Picture}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Let $H$ be a hereditary subset of $E^0$ such that the quotient $C^*(E \backslash H)$ is gauge-simple. Let $H'$ be the hereditary set
\begin{equation*}
H' = \{ w \in H \; \vert \; \text{There exists $x \in E^0 \backslash H$ such that $w \geq x$} \}. 
\end{equation*}
Then there is an isomorphism of Cu-semigroups
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}_E \cong \operatorname{Cu}_H \sqcup \; \big( \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'} \big).
\end{equation*}
On the RHS, if $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_H$, $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'}$ and $\rho: \operatorname{Cu}_E \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'}$ is the surjective Cu-morphism from Lemma \ref{lemma: Cu E Minus H} then $f + g = \rho(f) + g$ and $f < g$ if and only if $\rho(f) \leq g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'}$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Let $i_H: \operatorname{Cu}_H \rightarrow \operatorname{Cu}_E$ be the order embedding defined in \eqref{equation: Inclusion}. Recall that $i_H$ defines a Cu-isomorphism from $\operatorname{Cu}_H$ to the ideal $\mathcal{I}(I_H)$ of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. Define a map $\phi$ by
\begin{equation*}
\phi(f) = 
\begin{cases}
i_H^{-1}(f), \text{ viewed as an element of $\operatorname{Cu}_H$ if $f \in \mathcal{I}(I_H)$,} \\
\rho(f), \text{ viewed as an element of $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'}$ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
To see that $\phi$ is additive, assume that $f \in \mathcal{I}(I_H)$ and $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \backslash \mathcal{I}(I_H)$. By definition of addition on $\operatorname{Cu}_H \sqcup \; (\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'} )$,
\begin{equation*}
\phi(f + g) = \rho(f + g) = \rho(i_H^{-1}(f)) + \rho(g) = i_H^{-1}(f) + \rho(g) = \phi(f) + \phi(g). 
\end{equation*}
To see that $\phi$ is an order-embedding, assume that $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ satisfy $\phi(f) \leq \phi(g)$. If $f, g \in \mathcal{I}(I_H)$ then the inequality $f \leq g$ follows from the fact that $i_H$ is a Cu-isomorphism. Now assume that $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ is arbitrary and $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E \backslash \mathcal{I}(I_H)$. Then $\rho(f) \leq \rho(g)$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'}$ and by the Cu-isomorphism $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \cong \operatorname{Cu}_E / \operatorname{Cu}_{H'}$ (see Proposition \ref{proposition: First Iso Thm Cu E}) together with Lemma \ref{lemma: RPL Extensions}, there exists $h \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$ such that $\operatorname{supp}_0(h) \subseteq \langle H' \rangle$ and $f \leq g + h = g$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_E$. Hence, $\phi$ is an order-embedding. Finally, $\phi$ is surjective because $i_H^{-1}$ and $\rho$ are both surjective Cu-morphisms. Therefore, $\phi$ is an isomorphism of positively ordered monoids and we are done by Remark \ref{remark: POM Iso Between Cu Semigroups}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Observe that in Corollary \ref{corollary: Extension Picture}, $E \backslash H' = (E \backslash H) \sqcup (H \backslash H')$. Hence, 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'} \cong (\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H} \backslash \{ 0 \}) \oplus \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'}
\end{equation*}
and by Corollary \ref{corollary: Extension Picture}, we have a Cu-isomorphism
\begin{equation} \label{equation: Extension Picture Block}
\operatorname{Cu}_E \cong \operatorname{Cu}_H \; \sqcup \; \big( (\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H} \backslash \{ 0 \}) \oplus \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'} \big).
\end{equation}
We describe the addition and order on the RHS of \eqref{equation: Extension Picture Block}. Let $f \in \operatorname{Cu}_H$, $g \in \operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H} \backslash \{ 0 \}$ and $h \in \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'}$. Then $f + (g, h) = (g, \rho(f) + h)$ and $f < (g, h)$ if and only if $\rho(f) \leq h$ in $\operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'}$. The addition and order behave as usual when restricted to each disjoint component. \newline
\phantom{} \newline
An advantage the characterisation of $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ in \eqref{equation: Extension Picture Block} has over the one in Corollary \ref{corollary: Extension Picture} is the presence of $\operatorname{Cu}_{E \backslash H}$, which is isomorphic to either $\{0, \infty \}$ or $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ by Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}. These are the Cuntz semigroups of two (out of three) of the building blocks for unital graph C*-algebras. So with \eqref{equation: Extension Picture Block}, one can clearly see how the Cuntz semigroups of the three building blocks for unital graph C*-algebras combine to form $\operatorname{Cu}_E \cong \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E))$ when $E$ satisfies the standing assumptions.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Extension Dichotomy}
Let $E$ be a finite graph. The graph C*-algebra $C^*(E)$ is built by recursively taking extensions which are either direct sums or relatively purely large.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{definition: Saturation}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and $H$ be a hereditary subset of $E^0$. Define $H_0 = H$. Suppose that we have defined $H_n$ for some $n \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$. Define the set $H_{n+1}$ by
\begin{equation*}
H_{n+1} = H_n \cup \left\{ v \in E^0 \; \Big\vert \; 
\begin{matrix}
\text{$0 < \lvert r^{-1}(v) \rvert < \infty$ and} \\
\text{$r(e) = v$ implies $s(e) \in H_n$} 
\end{matrix}
 \right\}.  
\end{equation*}
The saturation $H_s$ is the set 
\begin{equation*}
H_s = {\bigcup}_{n = 0}^{\infty} H_n. 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
If $C^*(E)$ is gauge-simple then there is nothing to show. If $C^*(E)$ is not gauge-simple then there exists a proper, hereditary, saturated subset $F$ of $E^0$ such that the quotient $C^*(E \backslash F)$ is gauge-simple. Let $F'$ be the saturation of the hereditary subset
\begin{equation*}
F_0 = \{ w \in F \; \vert \; \text{There exists $x \in E^0 \backslash F$ such that $w \geq x$} \}.
\end{equation*}
Assume that $F' = \emptyset$. If $v, w \in E^0$, $v \in F$ and $v \geq w$ then $w \in F$. In this case, $F$ is an isolated subgraph of $E$ and $$C^*(E) \cong C^*(F) \oplus C^*(E \backslash F).$$ Now assume that $F' \neq \emptyset$. By Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph}, there exist a finite graph $E'$ satisfying the standing assumptions and a hereditary subset $H$ of $(E')^0$ such that $C^*(E') \otimes K \cong C^*(E) \otimes K$ and $C^*(H) \otimes K \cong C^*(F) \otimes K$. Observe that if $v \in F'$ and $v$ supports at least one cycle then by Definition \ref{definition: Saturation}, $v \in F_0$. Thus, if $v \in F' \backslash F_0$ then $v$ cannot support a cycle and subsequently, the applications of moves (S) and (CO) in the proof of Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph} remove all vertices originally lying in $F' \backslash F_0$. Consequently, the moves from the proof of Proposition \ref{proposition: Collapse Graph} transform $F'$ to the hereditary set 
\begin{equation*}
H' = \{ w \in H \; \vert \; \text{There exists $x \in (E')^0 \backslash H$ such that $w \geq x$} \}. 
\end{equation*}
So $C^*(F') \otimes K \cong C^*(H') \otimes K$ and by Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso} and Corollary \ref{corollary: Extension Picture}, 
\begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl}
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E)) & \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E')) \cong \operatorname{Cu}_{E'}
\\
& \cong & \operatorname{Cu}_H \sqcup \; \big( \operatorname{Cu}_{E' \backslash H'} \backslash \operatorname{Cu}_{H \backslash H'} \big)
\\
& \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H)) \sqcup \big( \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E' \backslash H')) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(H \backslash H')) \big)
\\
& \cong & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F)) \sqcup \big( \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash F')) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F \backslash F')) \big).
\end{IEEEeqnarray*} 
Finally by definition of $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F)) \sqcup ( \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash F')) \backslash \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F \backslash F')) )$ in Corollary \ref{corollary: Extension Picture}, $C^*(E)$ is purely large relative to the ideal $I_{F'}$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{definition: Inf}
Let $S$ be an ordered monoid. $S$ is said to be \textbf{inf-semilattice ordered} if for $x, y \in S$, the infimum $x \wedge y$ exists and for $x, y, z \in S$, $$(x + z) \wedge (y + z) = (x \wedge y) + z.$$
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{proposition: Cu E Inf}
Let $E$ be a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions. Then $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is inf-semilattice ordered. Hence, if $F$ is an arbitrary finite graph then $\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(F))$ is inf-semilattice ordered.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Assume that $E$ is a finite graph satisfying the standing assumptions and $f, g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. Define $f \wedge g$ to be the pointwise infimum of $f$ and $g$. By direct computation, $f \wedge g \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. The fact that $f \wedge g$ is the infimum of $f$ and $g$ follows from the fact that the order on $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is defined pointwise. To see that $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is inf-semilattice ordered, assume that $f, g, h \in \operatorname{Cu}_E$. Then
{\small \begin{equation*}
\operatorname{supp}_0((f + h) \wedge (g + h)) = \operatorname{supp}_0((f \wedge g) + h) = \big( \operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g) \big) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(h). 
\end{equation*}}
Now assume that $\check{v}$ is a terminal vertex for $(\operatorname{supp}_0(f) \cap \operatorname{supp}_0(g)) \cup \operatorname{supp}_0(h)$. Using that $\overline{\mathbb{N}}, \{ 0, \infty \}$ and $\operatorname{Lsc}(\mathbb{T}, \overline{\mathbb{N}})$ are all inf-semilattice ordered, we have that $$((f + h) \wedge (g + h))(\check{v}) = (f + h)(\check{v}) \wedge (g + h)(\check{v}) = (f \wedge g)(\check{v}) + h(\check{v}).$$ By Lemma \ref{lemma: Order Alternative}, $(f + h) \wedge (g + h) = (f \wedge g) + h$ and $\operatorname{Cu}_E$ is inf-semilattice ordered. The final statement follows from Theorem \ref{introtheorem: Cu E Iso}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lemma: Inf Pullback}
Let $A$ be a separable C*-algebra and suppose that $\operatorname{Cu}(A)$ is inf-semilattice ordered. Let $I, J \subseteq A$ be closed two-sided ideals of $A$. Then the following commutative square of $\operatorname{Cu}$-semigroups is a pullback square:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
\operatorname{Cu}(A/(I \cap J)) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \operatorname{Cu}(A/I) \arrow[d] \\
\operatorname{Cu}(A/J) \arrow[r] & \operatorname{Cu}(A/(I + J)). 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{corollary: Pullback}
Let $E$ be a finite graph and $H_1, H_2$ be hereditary, saturated subsets of $E^0$. Let $(H_1 \cup H_2)_s$ denote the saturation of the hereditary set $H_1 \cup H_2$ (see Definition \ref{definition: Saturation}). Then the following square is a pullback of Cu-semigroups:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash (H_1 \cap H_2))) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash H_1)) \arrow[d] \\
\operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash H_2)) \arrow[r] & \operatorname{Cu}(C^*(E \backslash (H_1 \cup H_2)_s)).
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
